#6698. The Milwaukee Brewers Are Stone-Cold Killers

There is something inherently funny about the way the Milwaukee Brewers, of all teams, finally won their first-ever World Series: in ruthless, cold-blooded fashion. This is the small-market, Upper Midwest, rust-belt team perhaps most famous, until now, for (1) a hat logo that everyone loves, (2) a sausage race and (3) a couple of baseball’s most notable clowns: the adored former player and broadcaster Bob Uecker, and the maligned former owner and Major League Baseball commissioner Bud Selig. Their manager, Pat Murphy—“Murph”—looks straight out of central casting for a sitcom about a Wisconsin dive bar. We’re talking about a ball club with some of the friendliest fans in sports, and whose team is among the most merciless in recent baseball history.

Just as the Brewers’ sense of timing has been perfect this whole postseason, these stone-cold killers even managed to dispatch the Tampa Bay Rays before Halloween. If you haven’t been paying attention, the Brewers have been praised by the baseball world all year long—even Derek Jeter said so—for playing baseball the “right way”: small-ball, teamwork, manufacturing runs, grinding away at every at-bat. Sounds romantic, right?

But what the Brewers have done is revealed what “the right way” actually looks: a bloodbath. And just like in any horror movie, they proved impossible to kill. They trailed games throughout the playoffs, including in every game of their relentless sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, in which the Brew Crew appeared to gradually suck the life out of the two-time defending champions.

For much of their existence, the Brewers have played second banana to the Chicago Cubs and St. Louis Cardinals, their division rivals. But even these rivalries are one-sided, as the Cubs and Cardinals save most of their hatred for one other. The so-called Border Battle between Milwaukee and the Minnesota Twins is one of Selig’s forced interleague rivalries, but it’s best viewed as a proxy, summertime, low-stakes feud between Vikings and Packers fans. Maybe what’s most promising is that an overlooked team has forged not just a winning formula, but a unique identity consistent with the club and its hometown’s unfussy reputation.

Much has been said of the Brewers’ playing style—but still not enough. They are an antidote to the turgid, individualist, power baseball of the 21st century. If the modern game has come to resemble an artillery barrage, in which teams are built around players selected for launch angle and exit velocity rather than strikeouts and batting average, the Brewers (not to mention the Rays) reached the Fall Classic by restoring a pitch-by-pitch knife fight. Nobody punishes teams quite like the Brewers. They battle at every at-bat, working the count and wearing down pitchers. Even with two strikes—no, especially with two strikes—they’re difficult to get out.

“They’re not worried about their own stats,” said the 67-year-old Murphy of his team during the trophy presentation. “No one cares about that.”

What does it look like when it all comes together? It looks like the fifth inning of Game 3in St. Petersburg, with the Brewers leading 2-0. With two outs and a runner on base, Christian Yelich, their aging captain and only full-fledged star, battled back from a ball and two strikes to draw a walk. The Rays brought in pitcher Cam Booser, who’d held opponents hitless with runners on base the entire postseason thus far. The Brewers, though, had other ideas, and what followed could be charitably described as a slaughter: Their next six batters all drove in runs before the Rays finally got another out. When the dust settled, Milwaukee was up 10-0. After two tight World Series games that could’ve gone either way, this was the knockout punch. Tampa fought hard to win Game 4 the following night in a 12-inning, bullpen-draining duel, but it was only a temporary reprieve, as Milwaukee’s pitching and clutch hitting meant the Rays could never really get going in the decisive game.

Apropos of their blue-collar image, the Brewers’ best players are largely self-made. Their ace, Jacob Misiorowski, is a lanky, 6-foot-7 second-round draft pick passed over by scouts for being too raw. The Brewers’ vaunted pitching lab, known for giving overlooked and overcooked pitchers an extreme makeover, turned The Miz into this year’s overwhelming Cy Young favorite in just his first full season, one in which he threw more 100-plus mile-per-hour pitches than anyone in baseball.

In the ABS era of refuting balls and strikes, their catcher, World Series MVP William Contreras, has perfected the challenge system. In one of the more entertaining sideshows of the postseason, Contreras honed his Terminator-like ability to read the strike zone better than the umpires themselves and regularly got balls turned into strikes, sometimes within eighths of an inch.

The team is rounded out by a devastating bullpen that includes Trevor Megill, who closed out Game 5. “10-year-old me would be so proud,” he said moments after winning, while holding a WWE-style championship belt.

Of course, the 2026 MLB season is now over, and with owners threatening a lock out until a salary cap is instituted with the next collective bargaining agreement, it’s tempting to wonder where this leaves baseball,. If the Dodgers’ success, enabled by their enormous financial advantage, is an argument for a salary cap, the Brewers’ win (and Tampa’s World Series appearance) would seem to refute it. Theoretically, couldn’t any team do this? Milwaukee is the small-market team that does everything right. They find market inefficiencies with a zeal that would make Malcolm Gladwell proud — when everyone was looking for home run hitters, they built a team out of smart drafting, savvy scouting and salvage opportunities, while avoiding the kinds of costly, long-term contracts that often cripple their rivals.

More likely though, the Brewers are the exception that proves the rule. A salary cap and floor won’t change the culture at big- nor small-market clubs governed by lousy owners who are apathetic about winning. It won’t turn poorly run organizations into well-oiled contenders. The owners who treat their ball clubs as private-equity bait, tax shelters and personal ATMs only want a salary cap for the huge increases in team valuations it is likely to produce, and it won’t magically compel some of them to turn their laughingstock franchises into dynasties that compete for pennants year in and year out.

In any case, credit the Brewers for seeing us out with a more sustainable vision. Nowadays, fans lament the loss of a two-strike approach, of situational hitting, of strikeouts. Yet these are the traits that brought a rust-belt ball club its first World Series title. Hopefully there’s a lesson there. If nothing else, the Milwaukee Brewers have left the game in a good place, and their maniacal tenacity sets the stage for baseball’s next big battle, not on the diamond but in the boardroom.

#6692. All About Joaquim Valente, Gisele Bündchen’s Husband and Father of Her 3rd Child

Supermodel Gisele Bündchen has entered a new era of her relationship with professional jiu-jitsu trainer Joaquim Valente. On Feb. 5, 2025, TMZ broke the news that the couple recently welcomed their first child. A day later, a source told People they had a baby boy.

Bündchen started dating Valente in June 2023, following her 2022 divorce from Tom Brady. Valente and Bündchen were friends before becoming romantically involved.

In March 2024, Bündchen confirmed that she and Valente were together. In an interview with The New York Times, she said, “This is the first time I am seeing someone that was a friend of mine first. It’s very different. It is very honest, and it’s very transparent.”

It was announced that they had married in December 2025.

So how did they meet...and how did their love story later begin? Ahead, a timeline of their relationship and everything you need to know about Valente.

According to People, Bündchen and Valente were together for over half a year before news of their relationship broke in February 2024.

“They’ve been dating since June. They’re taking it slow,” a source revealed. “They started out as great friends first. She’s very private about this and wanted to keep it quiet while they got to know each other.”

“They started out as friends,” a second insider told People. “He was a huge comfort for Gisele while she went through her divorce. Their friendship turned romantic after the divorce.”

“Joaquim is a great guy,” they added. “He is down to earth, kind, and inspiring. Gisele was hesitant about dating after the divorce. It’s been very natural for her to date Joaquim.”

Bündchen also “loves that he is Brazilian” like her, the source furthered. “They come from similar backgrounds. They both left Brazil very young. They have both created amazing lives for themselves in the U.S. They both love Miami, but also enjoy traveling. They both enjoy healthy living. Gisele’s in a great space. She is happy and very much enjoying life. Joaquim is perfect for her.”

Bündchen and Valente had happy news in late October. A source told People in a statement that Bündchen is pregnant with their first child together and her third. The source said, “Gisele and Joaquim are happy for this new chapter in their life, and they’re looking forward to creating a peaceful and loving environment for the whole family.”

A few days later, on November 4, People shared comments from a source saying Bündchen is “excited to embrace this new chapter openly.”

The insider added that the model has “received many positive messages and congratulations,” but “wanted to keep it private for as long as she could, doing so was starting to be a challenge.”

She “feels good” and is continuing “Pilates and other exercises that will help with birth too,” the source added. Bündchen has “always taken amazing care of herself,” and “eats healthy and meditates as well.”

The baby’s sex and birth date were kept private, but TMZ reported on February 5 that Bündchen “recently” gave birth to her and Valente’s first child. She and the baby are “healthy,” the outlet was told, and Bündchen is “super happy.”

On February 6, a source told People that they had a boy to whom they gave the middle name River. All of Bündchen’s children have water-themed nicknames.

Before they started dating, they were good friends who were photographed vacationing together multiple times.

Bündchen and Valente were seen going for a jog in Costa Rica in January 2023. A source shut down dating rumors then, saying “he’s been her kids’ jiu-jitsu teacher for years. There’s no truth to the rumors that they’re dating.”

On Nov. 16, 2022, photographs of Bündchen and Valente on a trip to Costa Rica came out, this time with her children—and his jiu-jitsu students—Benjamin Rein, then 13, and Vivian Lake, then 10.

Bündchen can thank her preteen son for her relationship with Valente. He is one-third of the Valente Brothers, and they are co-founders of a jiu-jitsu academy in Miami. In 2021, Bündchen signed her son up for classes at the martial arts school. After taking him to his first class and speaking with Valente, she decided to enroll herself.

On Feb. 23, 2023, Bündchen posted an Instagram Reel of her sparring in the Valente Brothers’ studio.

“I believe the more tools we have in our toolbox the better. I feel stronger, more confidence and empowered since I started practicing self-defense. I feel it’s an important skill for all, but specially for us women. Thank you @ValenteBrothers for being awesome teachers and for making training so much fun. I am looking forward to keep improving. Let’s go! 🤛🏼,” she wrote in the caption.

Valente has been studying jiu-jitsu since he was two years old.

In Bündchen’s March 2024 interview with the New York Times, she addressed rumors that she was seeing Valente before her divorce from Tom Brady, saying, “That is a lie.”

“This is something that happens to a lot of women who get blamed when they have the courage to leave an unhealthy relationship and are labeled as being unfaithful,” Bündchen continued. “They have to deal with their communities. They have to deal with their family. Of course for me, it just happens to be a little bit amplified.”

In 2007, Valente moved to Miami to study criminology at Barry University.

If you were hoping to get some Insta-stalking in, you’ll be disappointed. Valente does have an Instagram account, but he has it set to private currently.

On Wednesday, March 27, Bündchen was accompanied by Valente at the launch of her new cookbook, Nourish. It was their first public outing as a couple. In photos shared by Entertainment Tonight, Valente is chatting with guests at The Hub in Miami Beach, and Bündchen is speaking from the stage about the new book and some personal anecdotes.

One fan asked what meal she turns to after a “hard day or breakup.”

Later on, Bündchen thanked Valente and his brothers for teaching her about “food spacing and food combining.”

Bündchen and Valente signaled their relationship was still going strong in mid-June. They were photographed walking Bündchen’s dog together in Seaside, Florida, on June 15. They were affectionate in some pics, with their arms wrapped around each other. The couple was dressed casually, with Bündchen in a white tank top, cargo pants, and flip-flops. Valente wore a blue T-shirt, black shorts, and sneakers.

The couple was spotted riding water bikes near Bündchen’s home in Miami, with Valente seen snapping selfies. He was shirtless, wearing camouflage shorts and a navy hat, while Bündchen opted for a black bikini paired with an animal-print wrap. She finished the look with a large woven sunhat.

Bündchen and Valente enjoyed a romantic vacation in Costa Rica during their Thanksgiving holiday. Photos came out of the couple kissing on the beach, with Bündchen in a sheer white dress, which she wore over a black bikini. In other shots, they held hands. It marked one of their most affectionate appearances since news of Bündchen expecting her first child with Valente came out.

Bündchen was photographed taking a swim in Costa Rica with Valente on Christmas Eve, wearing a black string bikini that showed off her growing pregnant stomach. Her boyfriend and daughter joined her at some points as she strode through the waves.

On March 9, Bündchen and Valente were spotted on a yacht in Miami in their first sighting since news of their son’s birth came out in February 2025. Bündchen’s 12-year-old daughter, Vivian, also joined them. Bündchen wore a cheetah-print bathing suit with a black sarong, while Valente appeared to be steering the boat.

On March 13, Bündchen was seen in Miami with her infant, going for a walk with the baby strapped to her chest and her pet dog at her side. The model was wearing a white baseball cap, sunglasses, white tank top shirt, beige leggings, and white sneakers. The baby was held in a navy carrier and covered in a white blanket.

On March 22 and 23, Bündchen and Valente were seen kissing and enjoying a weekend on a yacht in Miami. On Saturday, Bündchen wore a black one-piece swimsuit with a wrap skirt, and on Sunday, she opted for a cheetah-print swimsuit with a black sarong. Valente kept it casual across both days in a black T-shirt and shorts.

Bündchen shared the first photo of her and Valente’s baby boy on Instagram. In the pic, the newborn rested on her shoulder in a white outfit that reads “I ❤️ Mom,” with his face turned away from the camera. The second photo features Valente, her two older children, and the baby, marking their first public appearance together as a blended family of five. In her caption, Bündchen reflected on motherhood, her time offline, and the loss of her own mom last year. She wrote, “Lately, I’ve been embracing the slower rhythms, the real connections, the beauty in the lessons that come with being present. Today, on Mother’s Day, I specially miss my mom, but my heart is full.”

On July 23, 2025, Bündchen posted on Instagram for the first time in nearly two months to celebrate her 45th birthday. The carousel included new photos of her and Valente’s baby boy: one showed her carrying him in a baby carrier on a walk, and another featured his footprint stamped on a birthday card that read, “Feliz Aniversário Mamãe!!!”

In her caption, Bündchen wrote, “Haven’t been around here much, but I wanted to take a moment to say thank you for all the warm birthday wishes. I’m so grateful for another trip around the sun and even more grateful to have spent it in nature, surrounded by love and my family. Today is also my mom’s birthday. We miss her deeply, but we know she’s always with us. I continue to trust and welcome life with an open heart, holding gratitude for all that is still to come.”

On November 8, Bündchen celebrated Valente’s birthday by posting an image of them walking hand-in-hand on the beach as the sun went down, the model carrying their son. She set the image to the song “Love Love” and captioned it, “Happy birthday @joaquimvalente! I love you!”

People reviewed marriage records revealing Bündchen and Valente got married on Dec. 3, 2025 in Surfside, Florida. TMZ reported that they had their ceremony at home.

In January 2026, Bündchen shared photos reflecting on the start of the new year, prompting speculation about her baby son’s name. In one image, Bündchen appeared wearing a necklace featuring initials associated with her family. The piece featured a “B” for her son Benjamin, a “V” for her daughter Vivian and a “J” for her husband, along with another letter—an “A”—that was partially covered by her hair.

Bündchen did not reference the initial directly in her Instagram caption, instead writing, “As the new year unfolds, my heart is full of gratitude for the moments spent recharging with my family. May this year bring you love, health, peace, and new adventures. May you find the courage to honor your heart’s calling and to know and love yourself more deeply. Wishing you endless blessings and a beautiful journey ahead. Here’s to making 2026 a truly joyful and meaningful year. Sending so much love.”

In January 2026, Bündchen marked her son’s first birthday with an Instagram, including photos of Valente spending time with their son. Reflecting on the milestone, Bündchen wrote in the caption, “I can’t believe it’s already been over a year since you came to bless our lives. Thank you, God, for so much❤️ 🙏.”

In a new carousel of pictures shared on July 18, Bündchen shared photos with Valente from her trip with him to Tahiti. In the images, her son can be seen enjoying the water with his parents and dancing.

She also included a cute shot of Valente introducing their son to a manta ray.

On October 29, Bündchen and Valente stepped out together for Lotus House’s annual charity gala in Miami. The Halloween-themed event, titled “Sparkles and Costumes,” was a special occasion for the supermodel, who received the organization’s It Takes a Village award alongside fellow model Karlie Kloss. Both women were recognized for their hands-on support of Lotus House, a shelter serving women and children.

The couple seemed to coordinate their costumes for the occasion, embracing country-inspired looks, with Bündchen wearing braids under a cowboy hat, with a plaid shirt and jeans. Valente complemented her outfit in a tan shirt, brown vest, jeans, and a buckle belt.

#6691. Wales Bonner and Adidas Are Still Cooking With Gas

Just over a year ago, Grace Wales Bonner was announced as the next creative director of men’s ready-to-wear at Hermès. The move made history, making the superstar British designer the first Black woman to lead a European luxury house; her hotly anticipated first collection is set to debut in Paris in January. It was quickly confirmed that even as Wales Bonner stepped into her role at Hermès, she’d continue to work on her beloved namesake label. What was slightly less clear is if her new position would have any effect on Wales Bonner’s ongoing collaboration with Adidas, one of the most fruitful partnerships in sneakers. But in the months since the Hermès announcement, the partnership has hardly slowed down. If anything, it’s only continued to cement itself as the gold standard for linkups between fashion houses and athletic brands. And this week, the duo drops its latest collection, another killer mix of new silhouettes and luxed-up favorites.

For fall-winter 2026, Wales Bonner and the Three Stripes are bringing the BW Army and Gazelle into the fold. Neither model has received the Wales Bonner treatment just yet, though the timing is just right for the former. The BW Army has been a sleeper hit in 2026 and designers like Wales Bonner riffing on it will only serve to further elevate its profile. Her take on the OG military runner swaps trades its typical smooth leather for paneled pony hair and croc-printed leather. It comes in two colorways—a simple black and a burnt gold with rich maroon interior lining.

The rest of the collection features some more familiar faces, including the Gazelle, Adizero Adios, and Wales Bonner’s signature Karintha silhouette. The latter comes in croc-stamped leather with gold-brushed eyelets, which calls to mind the designer’s beautiful navy blue Sambas from a couple years back. On the techy Adizero Adios, Wales Bonner paired an off-white suede construction with exaggerated stitching and a royal blue interior. Rounding out the group is the Gazelle in a similar colorway to the Karintha: croc-printed leather with an off-white tongue and heel tab, plus a gum sole and a royal blue lining.

Alongside the shoes, Wales Bonner cooked up some of the sleekest Adidas apparel we’ve seen this year. There’s a blue jumper inspired by football kits, long a staple of the collaboration, plus a boldly striped sweater in tones of auburn, brown, and red. The designer’s takes on Adidas tracksuits remain as flawless as ever, with this collection adding a navy blue pinstriped short version to the canon. The true highlight of the clothes offering, however, is a leather zip-up blouson in a rich dark brown with Adidas stripes down the arms.

The fashion world is waiting with bated breath to see what Wales Bonner delivers at Hermès, with all the resources of a historic maison at her disposal. For now, though, we’re just stoked that the new gig doesn’t seem to have abated her deep love for true-blue sportswear one bit.

#6688. Boyedoe Lagos Spring 2027

Across several African nations, fashion plays a significant part in shaping ceremonial attire. Ghanaian designer David Kusi Boyedoe is reimagining how heritage and culture can exist in today’s world. For spring 2027, he was heavily influenced by the Asante Kingdom, a Ghanaian ethnic group, and their dynamic relationship between an Asante King and the Asante man. “It’s also a return to our ideology, which is about going back and restoring, and making known our silhouettes,” he said. With this collection, titled ‘Oath’ (or ‘Ntam’ in Twi, a Ghanaian language), Boyedoe is swearing a pledge to his craft.

Often, there’s a monolithic perception of African fashion: it’s either experimental and bold or lacking commerciality to the Western world. But there’s a cohort of African designers that are offering a counter perspective, and Boyedoe is one of them. “Instead of creating a spectacle, I’m focused on designs that sell,” he said. Even though this collection is more commercially-driven and wearable, there’s still an interesting story rooted in culture, community, and craftsmanship—particularly as the majority of his pieces are handmade by local artisans in Ghana.

Overall, this collection wasn’t about spectacle. Upcycled denim, sourced from textile waste dumped in Ghana, was reworked into his signature patchwork design. Standout looks included a mini patchwork dress and a pair of barrel jeans paired with an off-white blazer. The denim was another avenue into accessories in the form of medium-sized patchwork bags. Boyedoe also introduced a new earthy color palette in silhouettes like an ivory coat and a moss green suit.

#6687. Inside the Underground Harry Styles Hospitality Network

It remains one of Gillian Harmon’s great pop culture regrets that she never got to see One Direction live. The 26-year-old is from Irvington, a small town in Mobile, Alabama, where major artists rarely make so much as a pit stop. “I think the closest they came was either Atlanta or New Orleans,” she says, though at the time Harmon was too young to make the trip across state lines on her own.

A year ago, she moved to New York City, which is more frequently graced with the presence of pop stars. Especially these days, as Harry Styles performs a 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, with fans coming from all corners of the world to attend. But Harmon, who lives on the Upper West Side, had something many of them don't: an apartment with a spare bedroom. So, in the spirit of fandom and hospitality, she figured she could give someone else the experience she wished she had and started inviting out-of-state Styles fans to crash—for free.

Harmon isn't the only one. Around the city, a small hospitality network has emerged among Styles devotees, with fans opening their apartments to strangers traveling to New York to see the residency. They offer up their couches, guest rooms, and even subway directions, acting as something closer to a tour guide than a host. For fans coming from places where seeing Styles requires a flight, hotel, and a considerable financial commitment, their generosity can make a huge difference. To these fans, seeing Harry Styles in concert is not a luxury. It's an inalienable right.

When tickets for the MSG residency went live this past January, not all New York-based Harry fans were feeling so magnanimous. Some fans who couldn’t get tickets complained of tourists swooping in and snatching them up. Harmon, however, saw an opportunity. If fans were coming all the way to New York City to see Styles command the stage in a rotation of business casual get-ups while singing the hits from his four solo albums, she could help ease the financial burden. When she posted a TikTok offering her spare bedroom to roving fans, the response was immediate. More than halfway through the residency, she has already hosted four people, with more scheduled to arrive for Styles’ final run of shows. Her roommates, who aren’t particularly devoted Harries themselves, were game. After all, they are used to Harmon's adventures in popstar-chasing, and they liked the idea of meeting new people.

Harmon gave priority to people who told her it was their first chance to see Styles, particularly those coming from places where the cost of both travel and accommodations would have been difficult to absorb. When too many fans wanted room and board for the same dates, she would simply spin a wheel.

The arrangement has made Harmon’s five-bedroom apartment a kind of accidental commune. She has personally shepherded some of her guests to the Garden by subway, shown first-time visitors how to navigate the city, and met up with them post-concert to debrief. They’ve gone to pop-ups, ridden boats in Central Park, and explored Roosevelt Island. “It was really wholesome,” Harmon says.

She has experienced the financial and logistical hell of trying to attend a Harry Styles concert firsthand. Harmon has traveled to Nashville for Styles shows herself, sometimes with friends from college, and has been scammed trying to get tickets. She remembers the humbling experience, later, of unknowingly buying bad seats. But she was grateful just to be in the building. The MSG residency marked her fifth time seeing him live. And she recently watched her best friend, who flew from Alabama for his first-ever Styles concert, have the time of his life in the pit.

It’s fitting that friendship has become part of the Harry Styles fan experience. During the 32-year-old’s Wembley show in June, he announced that “being somebody’s friend is the most incredible, beautiful thing you could possibly be to someone.” Throughout his solo career, Styles has returned to the intimacy of friendship as both a thematic linchpin and guiding philosophy: the people you find, the people who stay, the people who make an otherwise lonely life a little less so. Fans have especially latched onto the motto "Treat People with Kindness,” from the Fine Line track of the same title. “They’re happy,” Harmon says. “They’re positive, uplifting, encouraging.”

Across town, 32-year-old Carolina Sanchez saw Harmon’s video and got inspired. Originally from Mexico, Sanchez has been a Styles fan since he was first discovered on X Factor in 2010 and later moved to New York. When she saw a slew of comments from eager fans needing a place to stay under Harmon’s videos, she offered up her own two-bedroom in Staten Island.. Soon, messages came pouring in.

“I just want to be part of something special,” Sanchez told me. Her first guests arrived in early October. At first, Sanchez admits, the idea of allowing strangers into her home made her nervous. But she started vetting prospective guests on Instagram and getting a sense of their connection to Styles and his music. Eventually, she created a Google form asking for basic information and identification to make sure the person she had been speaking with was the person who arrived her the door.

Her husband was initially surprised by the arrangement but understood the compulsion. He had seen firsthand how expensive Sanchez’s own ticket to the concert was. If hosting another fan meant someone could put that money towards a ticket of their own, Sanchez wanted to help. Now, her husband is cleaning their guest room and putting together goodie bags for the people staying there.

Sanchez hopes the connections will last beyond the residency. She imagines visiting some of the women she meets on future trips, including one who is coming from Florida. The idea, she says, is to make friends and treat other people well. In the process, she is also making New York feel a little less like a city of strangers. “When I've told people what I was doing, they're like, Are you insane? Are you crazy?," recounts Zaia Rodriguez, one of Sanchez’s lucky guests. “I think part of it is stan culture; we make these connections on the internet with absolute strangers, and we talk to these people so often, we bond over the things that we love, and we become friends.”

For other fans, the journey is a little more complicated. Maria Miglio, a 29-year-old surgery resident from just outside Detroit, flew to NYC with a coworker and stayed a 15-minute walk from MSG. The hotel was $500-a-night, and tickets to the concert set her back another $200. Residents in Miglio’s program get only four days off each month. She flew out Friday after work and was back in Detroit by Sunday.

“Concerts are just such a community-based thing, especially for me,” says Erowyn Walsten, a 20-year-old student at the Fashion Institute of Technology. For her, the neighborly instincts demonstrated by Styles devotees are innate to One Direction fandom. She attended her first 1D show when she was nine, and even had a Harry Styles doll; he was always her favorite. She saw him again at 16, and is now preparing to go to MSG alone, where she expects to make friends, like she has at other concerts.

“I really think that honestly, as long as I've even been a Directioner, it truly felt like a family,” she says. The fandom’s largely female community, she believes, has made it easier to form lasting connections with people who are, ultimately, total strangers. Some of her closest friendships have grown out of mutual acquaintances met through Styles. “I think it's one of the most beautiful things,” she says.

The residency has also given the Garden a particular significance, the same way it’s Mecca for fans of the New York Knicks. Styles has called the venue “Harry’s House,” a phrase that has stuck with devotees. Cara McDonald is planning to fly from Ireland for the historic residency, the longest single-engagement run in the venue’s history, even with the steep price of hotels and flights. But she’s been saving up. Like Walsten, Mcdonald’s first concert was One Direction, giving the trip a certain emotional resonance. Even the cost of attending has become part of the story: McDonald’s resale pit ticket for the residency cost more than the ticket she bought for his previous tour in Los Angeles. But that's her primary indulgence, she says. “Concerts and rent, that’s it.”

There’s also a sense that this moment might be more fleeting than it seems. In a September 9th email to fans, Styles wrote that he “doesn't know what comes next,” a line that sent fans online into a frenzy of speculation. For those old enough to remember the collective emotional whiplash of One Direction’s indefinite hiatus announcement, there’s a particular appeal in making the trip now, while there's still a chance.

#6680. 23 of Heidi Klum’s Most Iconic Halloween Costumes Through the Years

Her severed hand costume is just the latest jaw-dropping one in her history.

No one does Halloween quite like Heidi Klum. Since 2000, the supermodel has been throwing yearly Halloween parties where celebs gather to mingle and have fun. Just as exciting as her annual bashes, however, are the truly over-the-top costumes she dreams up. Each year, Klum arrives in a costume more elaborate and incredible than the last—it’s truly a sight to see.

Ahead of Halloween, we took a walk down memory lane and rounded up some of the legend’s most memorable costume ensembles throughout the years. From adorable recreations of cartoon characters to fantastical superhero outfits, here are some of our favorites.

For her first-ever Halloween party, Klum wore a striking leather outfit that included a black wig, spiked collar, and knee-high boots. Her red lips and voluminous lashes were also nice touches.

The supermodel pulled a Bianca Jagger and arrived at the function in 2001 dressed up as the 13th-century horse-riding legend Lady Godiva. Her all-white ensemble featured a silver sequined bodysuit paired with a long bleached blonde wig.

The stunning look was created by designer Marc Bouwer. Here, Klum smiles during a fitting for the creation.

In 2002, the star decided on an adorable Betty Boop costume with a strappy red dress, red stilettos, elbow-length gloves, and suitably extravagant makeup. Her Halloween party that year was held at Capitale restaurant in New York City.

She’s pictured here posing with her fellow Victoria’s Secret Angel, Karolina Kurkova, while at the festivities.

For her 2003 holiday fête, the supermodel chose a gold alienesque look which showcased a metallic headpiece and gold metal teeth.

Klum showed up to her bash dressed in a witchy red look that consisted of a waist-length red wig, voluminous pointed hat, bone accessories, and plenty of red eye makeup. The party was held at Marquee in New York City that year.

She wore another spooky look for her 2005 Halloween get-together held in Happy Valley, New York. It’s hard to recognize her between the gigantic black wig and the pointy fangs.

The model attended her 7th annual Halloween party dressed as the forbidden apple (snake headdress and apple dress included) from the biblical story of Adam and Eve. Her then-husband, Seal, showed up as Eve.

In 2007, she stole attention at her get-together dressed in a head-to-toe cat ensemble which consisted of a gray leotard, bedazzled collar, and lifelike whiskers. The party kicked off in Los Angeles that year.

She’s pictured here testing the look a few days before the festivities.

A few years later, Klum was photographed on the red carpet walking into her event dressed as a superhero. The super original look showcased towering platform shoes, an elbow-length red wig, and all-over purple sparkles.

Klum shocked everyone when she opted to wear a skintight costume that transformed her into a skinless body. To make the look even more convincing, she was wheeled onto the red carpet on a stretcher with a “surgeon” by her side.

She flashed a smile at the camera while getting fitted a month or so before the event.

For her 13th Halloween party, Klum had a team of designers custom make her Cleopatra costume. She offered fans a sneak peek ahead of the finished product.

Klum decided to travel into the future and show up to her 2013 Halloween celebration dressed up as a much older version of herself. She donned a gray wig, a walking cane, and a strand of pearls for the occasion.

Klum wowed partygoers when she chose an intricate and hyper-realistic butterfly costume for her 2014 event.

Here’s a closer look at her awesome face paint that year.

The supermodel pulled out all the stops when she arrived at her 2015 party wearing a Jessica Rabbit costume. Between the lacy red dress, purple gloves, and makeup, Klum looks just like the iconic character.

Klum worked with talented makeup artists to bring her look to the next level.

#6679. The Best Men's Crewneck Sweatshirt in 2026, According to GQ

There’s no such thing as ‘the best men’s crewneck sweatshirt,’ at least not in the objective sense. As tactile and quantifiable garments can be, the truth is it’s all open to interpretation, and comes down to personal taste (even if your personal taste sucks). That said… I do have some strong opinions on what makes a good sweatshirt and have tested too many to name. I grew up wearing cheap, serviceable sweats from places like Walmart. I’ve also invested in unreasonably heavy 24-ounce sweatshirts and became obsessed with the unyielding craftsmanship of Japanese reproductions that required rare loopwheel machines.

Through decades of experience, I’ve honed in on what makes a sweatshirt special. A good crewneck sweatshirt should be comfortable, and that all comes down to fabric and fit. The fabric, usually made of either a French terry or a brushed fleece, should be both dense and soft. The silhouette shouldn’t squeeze, but should be relaxed enough to layer over a T-shirt or even a button-up. I’ve also dialed-in on the things you should avoid, like when sweatshirts are too tight in the neck, especially as a guy with a thicker gullet for my frame. And I really hate when sweatshirts are too long. As a long-torso individual, you’d think this wouldn’t be a problem, but it’s something that feels endemic to the genre.

Now that I’ve given you a brief tour of the weeds, let’s get into what you came here for. Through rigorous research and far too much time on our hands, here’s what’s what in the world of crewneck sweatshirts.

Reigning Champ has been in the sweats game for generations, producing some of the absolute finest hoodies, sweatpants, and crewnecks around. When I was first introduced to the brand an unspeakable number of years ago, it left an impression on me. The idea that something so basic could be so good revealed to me that my base line for quality was much lower than I’d realized.

Though we here at GQ have adored their slim-fit crewnecks for years, Reigning Champ's more classic-fitting sweatshirt is one that will stay steady through the fickle fashion trend cycle. It's made with custom-knit midweight French Terry fabric, cut with a relaxed but clean fit, and sewn with super smooth flatlock seams to cut down on bulk. While most sweatshirts will opt for either raglan sleeves or set-in sleeves, Reigning Champ’s crewneck stands out for its unique construction that uses both techniques. The result is a more tailored set-in sleeve look at the front with raglan details at the back to give the wearer a freer range of motion.

The brand’s name alone sets high expectations, and in every aspect, Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt meets and exceeds them. While $125 isn’t by any means cheap, the stunning quality from the fabric to the fit and finish all equate to a sweatshirt that punches well above its weight class. If I really had to nit-pick, though, I'd like to see the color palette expand a little more, especially for such an essential piece of kit.

If your sweatshirt budget is decidedly smaller, your first stop should be Russell Athletic, the Alabama sportswear stalwarts who literally invented the crewneck sweatshirt way back in 1926. Almost a century later, they're still turning out the best bang-for-your-buck fleece crew on the market. It's got all the classic details that made Russell a household name: ribbing at the cuffs and hem, a V-insert collar, and a classic cut (size down if relaxed ain't exactly your thing).

The midweight 9 oz. fleece is pleasantly soft and warm, and it's moisture-wicking and breathable so if you run a little hot, it won't emphasize the sweat in ‘sweatshirt’. The thing I like most about Russell’s crewnecks is that they still fit like the vintage joints—but you don’t have to work yourself to death bobbing between vintage stores trying to hunt one down.

No list of the best crewneck sweatshirts would be complete without Champion's reverse weave joint in the mix. Todd Snyder’s legendary collab (see below) has got style and function down pat for the new-school, but the OG heavyweight pullover deserves a crown of its own. The sturdy cotton-poly blend is soft but will hold its shape after countless wash cycles (loungewear and pizza go hand in hand—residual stains do not). Fabric aside, the fit is just right: not too slim, not too baggy, and with slightly dropped shoulders to make your neckline really pop. We pick quality over quantity any day, but with this classic sweatshirt you get the go-to year-round layering piece for the fewest amount of dollar bills.

If you’re expecting a soft, motherly embrace, I hate to tell you this, but Champion’s iconic Reverse Weave sweats aren’t the softest. In fact, they’ve got a pretty rough hand. But don’t worry about that too much because that’s just straight out of the box. What you get in return is an unquestionably beastly durability. And the longevity you get out of them means they’ll only get softer and luscious with age.

You can’t ignore the impact that vintage clothing has on the modern fashion landscape, not just for the endless references and inspiration it gives designers, but also for the sheer explosion of secondhand style. Vintage-obsessed dudes like myself will search high and low for forgotten garments with esoteric details, from jeans left in abandoned barns to rare leather jackets tucked away in grandpa’s attic. And if you’re thrifting skills aren’t up to snuff or if coughing up the dough to a dealer is too big of a hit, the best thing to do is to look to Japan where they’re even more obsessed with reviving the grails of bygone eras.

While many repro brands deserve their flowers, I’m particularly keen on Buzz Rickson’s' interpretation of the perfect vintage sweatshirt. The fabric is made using ultra rare loopwheel knitting machines that knit the terry material methodically and slowly, using the natural tension of gravity to achieve a product that’s shockingly soft for its density. It also results in a fabric that’s totally seamless around the torso, an old-school detail that’s hard to come by but oh-so-satisfying once you do. The crewneck sweatshirt also features low-profile flatlock seams, tall ribbing at the cuffs and hems, and the throwback V-neck insert for easy donning.

HAVEN's Excel crewneck employs the label's telltale details like custom ribbing and underarm gussets for increased range of motion. But the star of the show has to be the fabric which comes from rare 1980s Azume knitting machines, lauded for producing low-tension French terry with unrivaled softness and character.

Lady White Co.'s methodical approach to jersey knits has brought them to the top of the heap not just for tees and sweatshirts, but for the entire wardrobe. It's mini crewneck uses custom-milled terry fabric that's cut to a flattering cropped silhouette and garment-dyed for depth.

Look, I'm just as surprised as you are that Gap's heavyweight sweatshirt is not only $70, but actually that good. It's legit heavy and will handily knock out other sweats in beefier weight classes, especially since you can often find it on a mega discount.

The kings and queens of American-made cotton fleece at Camber make their crewneck from a beefy 12-ounce cotton fleece with just enough elastic in the body panels to make it feel like a big hug. Plus you can get it in 11 colors.

Dyed one at a time by hand, each sweatshirt from the New York-based indie label Buckets is completely unique and certainly distinct from the droves of potassium-dyed, sun-faded, vintage-inspired sweats that have flooded the market in recent years.

NYC-based 3sixteen has built out a line of carefully dialed-in menswear, like this hardy crewneck made with a fleece that's, quote, "some of the heaviest available on the market." And yet it's the pockets, surreptitiously slipped into the side seams, that have us nodding in appreciation.

Known for its chef-approved T-shirts, Whitseville's reproduction sweats deserve equal praise for its heavy all-cotton fleece, tubular construction, and double-V gussets that reference rare vintage crewnecks.

Quince's 70-30 cotton-poly blend recalls vintage sweats of yesteryear, the kind that were as soft as they were durable and didn't break the bank. Its Everyday fleece crew ticks all the boxes.

There are levels to sweatshirts, as humble as they are. What we look for in high-quality sweatshirts comes down to fabric, construction, and fit. Sweatshirt fabrics should be soft, certainly, but many high-quality options are quite burly and stiffer than you'd think. Most of the time, that means the more material goes into the sweatshirt the longer it'll last. And if you're willing to commit to them, they'll get softer and more comfortable the more you wear and launder them.

Most garments are made by overlapping fabrics and sewing them together. That may be fine for a dress shirt, but sweatshirts are made of a thicker, knit fabric which can bulky and irritating when it's sewn like this. We like sweatshirts that are made with flatlock seams which are made by butting two fabrics next to each other rather than overlapping; the result is a smoother, flatter seam. On rarer occasions, some sweatshirts are made the old-school way on either tubular knitting machines or very rare loopwheel knitting machines which produces a sweatshirt without any side seams on the body. Garment nerds go gaga over this kind of detail, but it's by no means a requirement for a good sweatshirt.

Sweatshirt fabrics are typically made from terry cloth, French terry, or brushed terry. (If that sounds familiar, it's because terry cloth is the same stuff that's used to make bath towels.) Terry cloth features loops of yarns which are absorbent and insulating. But the main difference between your bath towel and your sweatshirt is that sweatshirts only have the loops on the inside of the garment. Often, those loops are either brushed or shorn to give the material a luxuriously fluffy hand.

Fit is always subjective, but classic-fitting sweatshirts will fit somewhat relaxed all-around and fall at the hips. Slimmer sweatshirts will fit better if you want to layer them under a jacket and look cleaner with slim-fitting pants. For a fit that's more of-the-moment, opt for a sweatshirt that's boxier and cropped to go with some high-waisted, baggy trousers.

The humble crewneck helped Steve McQueen evade capture in The Great Escape, cemented John Travolta’s heartthrob status in Grease, and made Eddie Murphy a badass in Beverly Hills Cop. Paul Newman, the patron saint of laid-back menswear, wore one religiously. And today, a roster of famous—and famously stylish—dudes still put their trust in it. The only difference now is that it comes in a rainbow of different colors and silhouettes, not to mention fabrics far beyond the staid French terry.

Like many menswear staples, crewneck sweatshirts were born from athletics and have transcended into everyday leisure. You could style a crewneck with baggy jeans and sick sneakers for a streetwear-leaning aesthetic, dive headfirst into a preppy look with a pair of chinos and loafers, or turn up the lounge-factor and double it up with some sweatpants and classic sneakers.

Like The Bachelor, we had a flock of hopefuls vying for our love. But instead of hot singles, we had to dole out roses to a gaggle of cozy sweatshirts. One by one, we got to know each sweatshirt, taking them out on dates (literally), and looking intently for rock-solid characteristics, flaws, and dealbreakers. We wore every sweatshirt like any other piece of clothing in our closets, styled them with our favorite pants, scrutinized their fits, put them through harsh laundry cycles, and repeated the whole process over again. What we ended up with is this A-team of great crewnecks, from budget options to luxurious upgrades, and everything between.

#6677. Fruché Lagos Spring 2027

It was an exciting summer for Frank Aghuno, founder and creative director of Fruche. After winning Berlin Fashion Week’s contemporary prize, Aghuno travelled some 3,000 miles to the German capital and held his first international showcase. Still riding that high, the Lagos-based designer was eager to bring the collection home and present it to his Nigerian audience.

This collection asked us to embrace our natural quirks and imperfections. At times, that took on a literal meaning; “handwork can be imperfect in its natural state,” he said, be it naturally occurring holes in the wood carved beads or imperfections from dyeing. “There are quirks everywhere, from the perfectly styled looks to the looks that are more twisted and knotted,” he said.

Inspired by Nigerian boarding school uniforms, gingham featured heavily throughout the collection and came in several iterations, including cotton gingham; aso oke (a Nigerian textile) gingham; beaded gingham; and adire gingham, a traditional resist-dyeing technique. While the silhouettes felt contemporary, traditional crafting techniques remained a key component. From the fabric to the local wood carving, Aghuno was keen to collaborate with artisans based in Nigeria. The cotton used was sourced from Katsina and milled in Nigeria. “Everything is sourced here, and every look was made around the country,” he said, adding that he searched high and low for the right team to help develop the collection (including discovering craftsmen on TikTok). “It just goes to show the richness of our culture and the work we are doing today,” he said.

Standout looks included a satin dress and shirt featuring hand-painted artwork by Aghuno’s twin brother Dricky, an artist based between Lagos and London. At the show’s end, we heard the final look before it appeared on the runway. A model wearing an outfit made out of wood-carved shells walked out as the music drew to a close. The crowd fell quiet as they perched up in their seats and listened closely to the soothing sound of the beads brushing against each other. It was the first time I’ve heard Lagos that silent.

#6676. The Best-Dressed Guest’s Guide to the Holiday Wedding Season

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Great dresses, fabulous accessories, and plenty of reasons to RSVP yes.

Gorgeous gowns, sleek stilettos, sparkling jewelry—there’s plenty to love about getting glammed up for a wedding. It’s a chance to have a little more fun with your fashion, whether that means wearing a more dramatic gown than you’d typically go for, trying a bold color rather than your usual neutrals, or finally breaking out those festive heels. Whether the invitation calls for a destination, beachfront ceremony or a cosmopolitan, black-tie celebration, there’s an art to dressing for the occasion while embracing your personal style.

And that’s why Bloomingdale’s is your go-to. From romantic florals and sweeping gowns to metallic heels, bold jewelry, and conversation-starting bags, there’s something for every kind of celebration. Ahead, 11 wedding guest finds so good you may even want to wear them for the holidays.

Moody florals feel especially right for a fall wedding, and Simkhai’s draped maxi matches the romance of a countryside estate or garden ceremony. This fluid, body-skimming silhouette is especially elegant; play up the deeper colors with burgundy heels and gold jewelry, or add a tailored blazer if there’s a chill in the air.

Make your bag the focal point with Cult Gaia’s sculptural olive-green clutch, complete with a wavy gold handle. The earthy color feels especially fitting for an outdoor wedding; pick up a floral-print dress in a similar shade, or pair it with butter yellow for a more unexpected color combination.

If there’s one shoe to have in your wedding-guest wardrobe, it’s a great gold sandal. Aqua’s strappy pair adds extra sparkle with crystal-trimmed buckles and a sculptural heel, making them a flawless match for everything from printed midis to black-tie gowns.

An asymmetric, off-the-shoulder neckline feels unexpected. The draped silhouette and uneven hem give it extra movement for a cocktail affair, especially when paired with sculptural earrings and barely-there heels.

A beach wedding calls for something a little more shell-ebratory. Simon Miller’s polished silver clutch has a playful seaside touch thanks to its sculptural shell shape and black tassel. It stands out against a silky slip dress or bold black gown.

Wedding guest dressing is the perfect excuse to bring out the statement earrings. Pair these BaubleBar chunky gold-and-blue studs with a simple one-shoulder dress for a minimalist cocktail look.

A black-tie invitation is your chance to fully send it, and this Amur gown delivers with dusty mauve silk, delicate lace appliqués, and romantic off-the-shoulder detailing. For an estate wedding or grand ballroom reception, add crystal earrings, a satin clutch, and a sleek updo to show off the neckline.

Loeffler Randall’s gathered leather design with gold ring detail keeps things understated but still has plenty of personality. Carry it with an evening gown or tailored suit for the big day, then bring it back out with jeans and a blazer for dinner.

A black-tie wedding invites a little sparkle. Jennifer Behr’s crystal-covered hoops bring the shine with a bold, rounded silhouette. Wear them with a strapless satin dress or a sharply tailored evening look, sweep your hair back, and skip the necklace to let the earrings catch everyone’s eye.

A printed floral slip dress is a stunning choice for a tropical destination wedding—especially one with an ocean view. Farm Rio’s fluid maxi looks beautiful with gold sandals and playful earrings.

Leave it to Jimmy Choo to make black heels feel anything but basic! With sheer floral lace, a pointed peep-toe, and a slender stiletto heel, these satin mules look especially gorgeous with a sleek column gown or silk midi for a formal evening wedding.

#6675. Queen Camilla Arrives in Antigua and Barbuda in a Meaningful Poppy Brooch

She’s gearing up for Remembrance Day on November 11

Yesterday afternoon, Queen Camilla joined King Charles III in Antigua and Barbuda amidst his state visit to the Caribbean, after he spent the last few days traveling solo around Guyana and the Bahamas.

As she made her arrival, Camilla wore a turquoise tunic dress paired with tan flats, but it was the pin fastened to her chest that added a meaningful touch, a styling choice she borrowed from her daughter-in-law, Princess Catherine.

On November 11, the United Kingdom will celebrate Remembrance Day, a holiday that honors armed forces members who have died in the line of duty. Traditionally, royal family members commemorate the day by wearing red poppies, a symbol for veterans’ organizations that originated from the war poem “In Flanders Fields.”

But while royals most commonly wear felt poppies, here, Camilla chose a golden brooch from the Royal British Legion poppy shop.

Notably, the piece beared a resemblance to one worn by the Princess of Wales at the Remembrance Sunday memorial service back in 2019. There, Kate wore the Codebreakers Brooch, which acts as a tribute to workers in signal intelligence, with the design meant to emulate the rotors of the Enigma machines used by Allied forces during World War II.

That particular brooch had a special significance for Kate, because her grandmother, Valerie Glassborow, served as a code breaker at Bletchley Park, where she helped decipher German messages during the Second World War.

Now, while Camilla appears to be sporting a slightly different style (hers features two diverging leaves on a golden stem), she’s following in Kate’s accessorizing footsteps for the holiday.

In fact, the queen consort seemed to favor the brooch so much, she chose to wear it with her two following outfits, too. We’ll be keeping an eye out to see how many more appearances it makes during the rest of the trip.

#6674. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed. Braiding is a perfect example: it is a process that has not materially changed in thousands of years, despite being one of the most popular hairstyles for millions of Americans and a significant part of the $270 billion salon services industry,” said Ohanian. “Yinka has introduced a novel technology to a traditionally manual and highly specialized professional service.”

Company description: L’Oréal Group has taken a stake in Indian personal care company Innovist. (Vogue Business reported on speculations back in March.) The company has a successful portfolio that includes Indian haircare brand Bare Anatomy, skincare brands Chemist at Play and Sunscoop, and bodycare brand Vinci Botanicals. The company was founded in 2018 by Rohit Chawla, Sifat Khurana, and Vimal Bhola with a focus on science-first formulations, transparent ingredients, and in-house research and development.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L’Oréal Group (portfolio includes: Cerave, La Roche-Posay, Vichy, Armani Beauty, SkinCeuticals).

Investor comments: “Our investment in this innovative Indian startup is a clear testament to our unwavering commitment to expanding L’Oréal’s footprint in India,” CEO Nicolas Hieronimus said. “By bringing together the very best of L’Oréal’s global expertise with Innovist’s high-performing, science-led products and deep-rooted understanding of the Indian consumer, I believe we are poised to shape the future of beauty in this dynamic market.”

Company description: Remedy is a dermatologist-developed skincare brand founded by Dr. Muneeb Shah in March 2024. The brand’s products target skin concerns such as dark spots, dryness, fine lines, dullness, keratosis pilaris, and sensitive skin. Remedy is stocked on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Target, the latter of which it partnered with in December 2025. The Series A investment will support the skincare brand with its next phase of growth, including advancing clinical research, expanding its product categories, and improving inventory. Remedy also plans to strengthen its formulation, testing, and consumer education.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L Catterton (portfolio includes: Merit Beauty, Tula, Kopari, Elemis, Nutrafol, Intercos, Ex Nihilo).

Investor comments: “We seek to partner with exceptional founders building brands that will redefine categories, and we believe Remedy is uniquely modernizing dermatological skincare,” L Catterton partner Tehmina Haider said. “As both a clinician and a consumer educator, Dr. Shah has built a portfolio of simple, effective, and accessibly priced products that leverage advanced ingredient technologies to address real patient needs — and that is what will define the next generation of dermocosmetics. The brand’s rapid growth reflects deep consumer demand for affordable, clinically-grounded skincare, and we are thrilled to partner with the Remedy team on its next chapter.”

Company description: Bacchus is a London-based PR agency founded in 1998 by Anouschka Menzies and Charlotte Lurot, who currently lead the business alongside co-CEO Daize Washbourn. The agency specializes in luxury hospitality and culture, as well as in the prestige VIC and high-net-worth communities. With around 100 employees across seven offices (London, New York, Miami, LA, Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha), Bacchus generates annual sales of approximately $17 million. Its client portfolio includes Red Sea Global Residences, Six Senses, Auberge Resorts, the Victoria & Albert Museum, and Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer.

Funding and round: Acquisition, majority stake.

Investor(s): Mazarine Group (portfolio includes: La Mode en Images, the show producer of Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Gucci).

Investor comments: “There were several objectives [with this investment],” Mazarine founder Paul-Emmanuel Reiffers tells Vogue Business. “First, we needed to add a public relations and influence branch to our group. Second, it had to be large enough for us to develop and accelerate it. With Bacchus, we’re starting from a platform that’s already large enough to consolidate operations, grow further, and open an office in Paris in the short to medium-term.
