Investor comments: “As a long-time supporter, I have witnessed Crown Affair consistently demonstrate the strength of its brand with a unique blend of elevated, clean haircare innovation, thoughtful hair rituals and authentic storytelling,” said Cristina Nuñez, co-founder and managing partner of True Beauty Ventures.

Company description: Beauty supplements and wellness brand, founded by influencer Tati Westbrook in 2018. Westbrook departed the company in August 2024 after settling a four-year legal battle in which her business partner, Clark Swanson, accused Westbrook and her husband of fraud, negligence and breach of fiduciary duty to Halo Beauty.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor comments: “We’re honoured to carry Halo Beauty’s legacy forwards by expanding its mission of clean, effective beauty and wellness. This acquisition marks a new era of innovation and commitment to empowering consumers with products that enhance both their beauty and overall well-being,” said the private investor.

Company description: Skincare brand known for peptide-infused anti-ageing products. The brand claims its signature OS-01 peptide can reverse the skin’s biological age ageing by preventing senescent or “zombie” cells, which are cells that are alive but damaged. OneSkin was founded by four PhD scientists: Carolina Reis de Oliveira, Alessandra Zonari, Mariana Boroni and Juliana Carvalho. The recent investment brings OneSkin’s total funding to $20 million.

Investor(s): Selva Ventures, Plus Capital, Unilever Ventures, Able Partners, Camila Alves McConaughey (Brazilian-American model and wife of actor Matthew McConaughey), tech entrepreneur Kevin Rose, plus previous investors.

Investor comments: “As a Brazilian woman, I am thrilled to invest in a brand founded by four Brazilian female scientists — my heritage is something I’m incredibly proud of, and I am honoured to support those who are executing this work. The OneSkin team has built a line of products that hold a unique space in the massive skincare market. I fell in love with the products the moment I saw the results on myself, and I knew I had to be a part of it! I’m so looking forward to seeing their future innovations and continued success with the help of this funding,” said McConaughey.

Company description: Wholesale vintage clothing marketplace founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal. The platform connects retailers and resellers to inventory from verified vintage wholesalers around the world.

Funding and round: £17 million total, £4.7 million in seed and £12.3 million in Series A.

Investor(s): HV Capital (portfolio includes: Depop, Zalando, Hello Fresh), Andreessen Horowitz (portfolio includes: Instagram, Pinterest, Roblox), Y Combinator (portfolio includes: Snap, Airbnb), Shopify president Harley Finkelstein, former Depop CEO Maria Raga.

Investor comments: “We are proud to invest in Fleek, a company that is redefining the secondhand fashion landscape. Fleek’s innovative approach to scaling the secondhand market globally reflects tremendous potential for growth. The marketplace not only addresses current industry needs but also paves the way for a more sustainable future in fashion. We’re excited to be part of this journey,” said Felix Klür, general partner at HV Capital.

Company description: Founded in 2005 in Stockholm by Jockum Hallin, Cristopher Nying and Richardos Klarén, Our Legacy is known for high-quality menswear with intricate design signatures. The brand has around 200 stockists and seven of its own stores, and has risen in notoriety thanks to buzzy collaborations with Stüssy and Emporio Armani.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Lead investor(s): LVMH Luxury Ventures (portfolio includes: Aimé Leon Dore, Lyst, Heat).

Investor comments: “Our Legacy is the epitome of what we could call the ‘quiet cool’ tendency, featuring a unique blend of contemporary minimalism and creative subversion,” said Julie Bercovy, CEO of LVMH Luxury Ventures Advisors.

Company description: Californian premium athleisure brand Vuori was founded in 2015 by Joe Kudla. The brand is known for its unique fabrics and is certified as carbon neutral by Change Climate. Following this investment, the brand’s valuation has reached $5.5 billion, building on a $400 million investment by Softbank Vision Fund 2 in 2021, which brought its valuation to $4 million.

Funding and round: $825 million, secondary tender offer.

Lead investor(s): General Atlantic (portfolio includes: Gymshark, Sézane, Tory Burch), Stripes (portfolio includes: On, Reformation, Khaite) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “Vuori encapsulates everything we look for in a Stripes investment — the products are amazing and beloved by the consumer, the team is fanatical about quality and innovation, and the market for athleisure is global with durable tailwinds,” said Chris Carey, partner at Stripes.

Company description: Secondhand peer-to-peer marketplace founded in 2008 by Milda Mitkutė and Justas Janauskas in Lithuania. The platform is Europe’s largest clothing resale marketplace. The recent investment brings Vinted’s valuation to €5 billion.

Funding and round: €340 million, secondary share sale.

Investor(s): TPG Tech Adjacencies, Hedosophia (portfolio includes: Monzo, Go Puff), Baille Gifford, Invus Opportunities (portfolio includes: Coupang, Chrono 24), FJ Labs (portfolio includes: Farfetch, Uber, Klarna), Manhattan Venture Partners (portfolio includes: Discord, Epic Games, X), Moore Strategic Ventures.

Investor comments: “We’ve seen that consumers are increasingly choosing secondhand as a core part of their wardrobe, as sustainability and flexibility become top of mind for many people. Vinted’s customer focus, leading product experience, and sophisticated approach to logistics have made this market accessible to an even broader population,” said TPG partner Andrew Doyle.

Company description: Biotech-powered prestige skincare brand Reome was founded by beauty editor and acupuncturist Joanna Ellner in 2023. The UK-based brand is known for its sensorial products and is stocked in Space NK, Liberty and Moda Operandi among others.

Investor(s): Rianta Capital (portfolio includes: El Rayo, Home Cooks).

Company description: UK-based women’s shirt brand launched in 2017 by a former Vogue stylist and Tatler editor Pip Durell. The B Corp-certified brand, which is known for timeless designs inspired by men’s tailoring and British heritage, launched its first pair of trousers earlier this year and plans to expand further with blazers and knitwear at the start of 2025. With Nothing Underneath was named one of Walpole’s Brands of Tomorrow in 2022.

Lead investor(s): Pembroke VCT (portfolio includes: Tala, Me+Em, Bella Freud) and JamJar Investments (portfolio includes: Deliveroo, Oatly, Spoke).

Investor comments: “With Nothing Underneath (WNU) holds a unique position in the womenswear market. Pip and her team have built a fantastic brand around one staple item, the shirt — an essential in most women’s wardrobes. It has become a standout in the fashion industry and early growth metrics have given us conviction in the brand. This investment will enable this emerging British heritage brand to enhance its product range, assist with growth and support WNU’s international reach,” said Andrew Wolfson, CEO of Pembroke Investment Managers.

Company description: UK-based luxury retail platform that stocks a curation of independent brands. The retailer is known for its selection of vibrant eveningwear. Founded in 2019 by Nina Briance, Cult Mia initially received $3 million in seed funding in November 2023 led by Fuel Ventures, with participation from Morgan Stanley and David Wertheimer of the Chanel family.

Funding and round: $2 million, seed (bringing total seed funding to $5 million).

Investor(s): H&M Group Ventures (portfolio includes: Goop, Klarna) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “We are delighted to invest in Cult Mia on their mission to launch independent and diverse designers from around the world. We have been incredibly impressed by all that Cult Mia has achieved in such a short space of time,” said Nanna Andersen, chief of new growth and ventures at H&M Group.

Company description: Founded in 1997 by Dr Gregory Brown, Révive is known for its luxury serums and creams powered by bio-renewal technology. The brand was previously acquired by Shiseido in 2016, before it was sold to Tengram Capital Partners in 2017.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): S’Young Group (portfolio includes: Evidens de Beauté, Pier Augé).

#6672. Kendall Jenner Recreated a Cult-Favorite ’80s Movie Look for Halloween

With a November 3 birthday, Kendall Jenner started the celebrations early. The model threw a party on October 30 to fête Halloween and turning 31.

On October 31, she shared photos of her costume. The model transformed into Jane Henderson, the character played by Nastassja Kinski in Wim Wenders’s 1984 film Paris, Texas. The model traded her signature brunette hair for a chin-length platinum-blonde bob. She paired the look with a fuzzy, low-back hot pink minidress and sheer black tights. In one photo, she channels a memorable scene from the film, posing at a bar.

For those unfamiliar with the reference, Paris, Texas follows Travis Henderson, a mysterious drifter who reappears after four years away and attempts to reconnect with his young son and estranged wife, Jane. Directed by Wenders and written by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Sam Shepard, the film is considered one of the German filmmaker’s most celebrated works. It took home the Palme d’Or at the 1984 Cannes Film Festival and has since earned cult film status. More than four decades later, its imagery remains recognizable to cinephiles and fashion fans alike.

Jenner wasn’t alone in her cinematic costume. Actor Jacob Elordi joined her as Travis Henderson, the character portrayed by Harry Dean Stanton in the film.

While it marks the rumored couple’s first costume together, it’s not the first year Jenner has thrown a birthday party during Halloween weekend. In 2019, she teased that she was “keeping the Halloween birthday party alive for mom” on Instagram.

This year’s bash, which was thrown at Bar Marmont in Los Angeles, had a star-studded guest list. Attendees included Charli XCX, Hailey Bieber, Laura Harrier, and more.

#6671. The Best Men's Jean Jacket 2026: 12 Fall Layering Essentials

Adding the best men's jean jacket to your closet is like drafting Lebron to your rec league team: you’ll end up with a ‘ship no matter how bad the rest of the squad is. Whatever you want to call ’em—jean jackets, denim jackets, trucker jackets—the all-American stalwarts are the layering MVPs of every outfit on the brink of an L. Makes sense considering blue jeans, the jacket’s southern equivalent, can do the exact same thing for your wardrobe. Workwear roots bestow the humble piece of outerwear with utilitarian features, durability, and classic proportions—a surefire formula that churns out menswear icons like double-knee pants and chore coats.

What started out as a work jacket to accompany the blue jeans made from the same burly denim material, jean jackets have grown out of their pragmatic uniform and are more of a fashion statement these days. Be it a luxurious runway riff, an upgraded take, or a down-home workhorse, every flavor of denim jacket has the potential to make every outfit pop. Of course, the trucker jacket is what comes to mind first. But denim jackets come in many forms and aren’t limited to the Levi’s version you likely have in your mind’s eye. Denim’s enduring appeal and boundless applications have seen it merge with chore coats, trenches, Harringtons and more, expanding the scope of jean jackets. That’s great news for anyone looking to find one that truly speaks to themselves, but terrible news for anyone attempting to wade through all the options.

So we did the denim digging for you. We went out and scraped the market for the absolute best men’s jean jacket, from the tried-and-true to the new-age startups and everything in-between.

This shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone. And if it is, as this company’s self-proclaimed Denim Guy, it’s definitely my fault for not teaching you. Levi's is the grand daddy of all jeans which puts them on a rarified level few others could ever hope to approach. The brand’s iconic 501 jean gets most of the (deserved) praise, but the Levi's trucker jacket also warrants recognition.

The very first iteration of the Levi's trucker jacket debuted in 1905 and has since gotten several updates, but the one most ubiquitous today is known as the Type III. It's the picture you have in your head when you think of a trucker jacket and it's great for so many reasons. The midweight denim is ideal for year-round wear, the trim and cropped silhouette has transcended trends for decades and, like the five-pocket blue jean, pairs with just about everything (and looks better the more you wear it). If you only have a hundred bucks to spare and enough room for just one denim jacket in your rotation, it had better be this one.

A chore coat isn’t what most people think of as a ‘jean jacket’. But I’m proposing this as a more practical, no-less stylish alternative to the usual trucker jackets you’re used to seeing. And if you’re taking the term ‘denim jacket’ liberally, any outerwear made of denim would count. Anyway. Chore coats are more commonly made of a sturdy canvas or heavy moleskin cotton fabric, but denim's resilience make it another reliable option for the workwear genre. It doesn't get much better than this one from Alex Mill.

The brand's range of modern menswear staples is no slouch when it comes to fabric and construction and its line of chore coats is among the best out there, even compared to the multi-generational stalwarts like Carhartt and Dickies. This one’s made with sturdy, yet broken-in 100% cotton Japanese denim and comes with dual chest pockets and hand pockets, not to mention a stealthy phone pocket. The relaxed fit borders on boxy and is roomy enough to layer over a sweater or thick hoody once the temps drop. But if you're not the denim type (why are you even here?) Alex Mill makes its work jacket in a range of different fabrics, too.

To me, Alex Mill’s chore coats are nearly perfect. They fit like a dream and come with just the right vintage details that make guys like me swoon. I’ve compared it with my vintage French chore coat and not only are the details almost identical, the craftsmanship is virtually the same. So you could search for hours for a vintage one, or you could save the time and money and just get Alex Mill’s.

Levi’s may be the dominant denim trucker jacket, but they aren’t the only ones with a classic trucker jacket etched into the annals of menswear history. Lee’s left an indelible mark on the American denim landscape and is rightfully considered one of the so-called Big Three along with Levi’s and Wrangler. Lee’s famed Rider jacket was first introduced in 1948 and is considered one of the best denim jackets of all time.

Today’s modern reproduction is made by the brand’s retro sub-label, Lee 101, and features the same left-hand twill denim the brand is famous for, this time woven by a storied Japanese denim mill. The signature zig-zag stitching details at the collar and front placket still remain, as do the cateye buttons at the waist, and the slim, hip-length silhouette. If you’re hardcore, I’d recommend you go with the raw denim version and earn those fades yourself. But if you can’t be bothered to put in the work for five years straight, then stick with the light wash version.

Fans of the Japanese brand Kapital are quick to point out the brand's head-spinning takes on denim. From painstaking boro patchwork stitched by hand to far-out interpretations of blue jeans, the cult-loved label is a true innovator in the denim space. Its catalog is chock full of certified grails, but if you’re focusing in on jackets, it doesn’t get any crazier than its boro jacket. From the outset, it looks more like an antique pile of fabric than a jacket—and that’s kind of the point. The jacket is made of dozens and dozens of fabric scraps, each one meticulously distressed—and then repaired— to look like worn-out vintage textiles before sewn back together as a single garment.

As you can imagine, the process is extraordinarily time-consuming. That immense dedication results in a jacket that’s truly not for the faint of heart or those with shallow pockets. This particular jacket takes inspiration from Type I denim jackets and features a single flap pocket, rear cinch, and a boxy cropped fit. It may look shredded, but putting it on feels like absolute butter thanks to the custom, boro-printed satin interior.

Kaptain Sunshine has long been known for its loving recreations of heritage American workwear, but the artful way it approaches its designs has earned it a ton of crossover appeal with the fashion crowd. Case in point: This one-pocket denim jacket, which is constructed according to classic selvedge standards, but has enough interesting details (including a buckle back) to inspire the envy of any runway show attendee. Wear it carefully—you never know which menswear nerd could be nearby and hoping to swipe it from your chair.

The circle of iconic denim jackets is small. Even so, there’s one that doesn’t get as much attention it ought, and that’s the Type II trucker jacket. Levi’s introduced the Type II in 1953, the long-awaited follow up to the Type I. The features were much the same, but the main difference was the addition of a symmetry-imposing second pocket and adjustable waist tabs instead of a cinch back. The result is one of the most geometrically pleasing jackets ever. The boxy fit and spare details are very much in line with workwear designs, but there’s something also very minimalist about it, too. No wonder it still gets referenced and duped by modern designers.

Levi’s will always be the OG when it comes to the Type II, but if you really want to get one, The Real McCoy’s is the one to get. The Japanese brand is known for going insane lengths to reproduce the most coveted and iconic pieces of vintage menswear and their rendition of the Type II is a prime example. The denim was designed from the ground up, using a specifically sourced vintage loom that was able to deliver the kind of slubby character of ‘50s denim at a consistent clip. The result is one of the most accurate reproductions you can get. That is, if you can even find it. Thanks to the limited fabric production and high demand, the jacket is so sought after that it’s been sold out for ages.

Don’t let Gap’s iconic khakis ads make you forget that the iconic brand got its start in denim. That DNA is still prevalent today as Gap’s stable of denim offerings is as strong as ever. Case in point, this faithful take on the famous Type II trucker jacket featuring knife pleats, dual chest flap pockets, and a boxy cropped fit—all done in a hearty all-cotton denim.

If we didn’t tell you, you might not realize this was denim too. But even though it's finished in soft corduroy, there's a full denim jacket inside, taking trompe l’oeil to a new level. While most attempts would easily fall flat in the uncanny valley, Jeanerica's result offers the best of both worlds (and textures).

Before Ralph launched his western-inflected RRL line, Polo was still making workwear hits. And denimheads could easily miss this pitch-perfect take on the Type II trucker jacket with its impeccable cut and spot-on vintage wash.

J.Crew and Lee's collaborative iteration on the denim jacket is a true sleeper hit, featuring a mix of details from a corduroy collar, trendy (and practical) plaid lining, and those beautiful, unmistakable Lee trucker pockets. This is the denim jacket to take with you into fall.

Ralph's premium ranch-hand line has been quietly making the best faded denim in America for decades: The 'Leeland' wash has genuine depth to it, and even better—the buttons are embossed with “Cowboy.”

Material and construction: With denim jackets and jean jackets, the most important factor will be the denim itself. Make sure that the denim feels substantial and weighty. Good quality denim shouldn’t be too thin or loosely woven. Though I personally prefer denim without any sort of elastane, you may want to consider opting for a jacket with some stretch built into it for ease of movement. Even then, I’d advise you to limit the percentage of stretch to no more than 2%. Selvedge denim and Japanese denim are often a good sign of a high-quality fabric, but non-selvedge and non-Japanese denim can be well-made too, so don’t put all your trust in provenance.

Fit: Fit is subjective, but most trucker jackets follow a tried-and-true formula with a hem that hits right at the hips. They may have a leaner silhouette or a boxier cut, but a hallmark of trucker jackets is truly the cropped length which helps emphasize your natural proportions and lengthens your legs (without having to spend tens of thousands of dollars and months of agony). Denim jackets with hand pockets are often a little longer than those without, so if you may want to factor that into your decision.

Silhouette: Sizing is key, as well. Most denim jackets are cut on the more tailored end and around hip length. Make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your shoulder bones if not a little past. Keep in mind that you may want to layer underneath, since that will affect how snug the jacket will feel. With time, the sleeves of a trucker jacket will tend to get shorter as the elbow creases set in so if the sleeves are a tad long, you’re probably in a good place.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6670. The Tragic Story Behind La Bola Negra, One of The Year’s Best Films

Based on an unfinished play by Federico Garcia Lorca, the movie is already garnering Oscar buzz

It is rare to come across uncompromisingly queer work from LGBTQ+ artists from over a century ago and beyond. Many writers did not get to see their work published in their own lifetime; E.M. Forster’s groundbreaking novel Maurice, which he began writing in 1913 and which featured a rare-for-the-time happy ending, was not published until a year after his death, in 1971; while Emily Dickinson’s romantic stanzas, which many critics believe were dedicated to her sister-in-law, Susan Gilbert Dickinson, weren’t even discovered until long after her passing. But even those queer artists that did see their work out in the world didn’t manage so easily. James Baldwin was told by his agent to burn the manuscript for Giovanni’s Room. Jane Rule was rejected over 20 times in her efforts to find a publisher for Desert of the Heart.

One of this year’s most critically-acclaimed films, La bola negra (”the black ball” in English), is based on an unfinished play of the same name written by the Spanish poet and playwright Federico Garcia Lorca in 1936. In the four pages of the story that remain, a wealthy young man is trying to gain entrance to an exclusive casino in Granada. In order to determine his admittance, the members turn to a voting system where they choose to roll a white ball in favor, or a black ball in opposition. After they vote, he is handed a black ball, and afterwards when his father asks him why he thinks he was rejected, the boy tells him that it’s because he is gay.

Tragically, Lorca never got the chance to finish what may have been a groundbreaking story. (He was shot dead by nationalist forces after being imprisoned during the beginning of the Spanish Civil War, and his remains have never been found.) But he had detailed his ideas for the drama in a letter to fellow playwright Cipriano Richas Cherif.

That’s where Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the directing duo endearingly referred to as “Los Javis,” comes in. Their movie rewrites a bit of history, making it so that Lorca (also a character in the film) manages to complete most of his play, save for the last few pages. The film jumps between three different years—1932, 1937, and 2017—to explore the lives of different gay men across a century, who are all loosely connected by the writer’s work. (The cast includes stars like Élite’s Miguel Bernardeau, folk-pop singer Guitarricadelafuente, and Oscar nominee Glenn Close.)

“We don’t have that many movies or books about the history that connects us as a community, the queer community,” co-director Ambrossi told NPR earlier this week. “That’s why we wanted to make it big. We wanted to make it epic and we wanted to make it bold.”

To try to piece together the story, the directors combed through old letters and archives to try to imagine how Lorca might have ended it. “We were like detectives,” co-director Calvo noted. “It was fun to discover that he would like to talk about his projects in parties.” And these pieces are precisely how the story of La bola negra came together (but don’t worry, no spoilers here).

Now, Los Javis are bringing light to this untold story in an effort to preserve queer history and maintain the legacy of someone who couldn’t so freely tell his truth.

“We are all connected by this black ball that we all share, that we pass to each other, every generation—a black ball, that is silence, pain, shame, but also it’s a spark of life and desire and love and joy,” Calvo says. “I feel like [this project] made me feel proud of my community and of the brave people that fought before me.”

You can watch La bola negra in theaters now. It arrives to Netflix on December 2.

And after spotting Kristen Bell carrying the iconic BaubleBar Custom Alpha tote customized with her initials (a style also vetted by Emma Roberts and Alix Earle, might I add!), I’m officially sold on getting one of my own. While out in New York City ahead of the premiere of her hit Netflix show Nobody Wants This, which she stars in alongside Adam Brody, Kristen Bell wore a simple yet elevated outfit featuring a white tee, blazer, jeans, pointed-toe heels, and a bag with her initials “KB” on it that gave the whole look an extra punch. The small size fits all the everyday essentials, plus a Kindle or a pouch for miscellaneous on-the-go items. Its canvas material also makes it a durable option for everyday use. And this updated version comes with a trolley sleeve, making it easy to slide over your suitcase handle when traveling!

As for customization, you can choose from 19 different tote colors and 13 letter colors to make it your own. You’re allowed up to three characters for your monogram, so you can go with your first, middle, and last initials, just your first and middle, or, if you’re like me and have a three-letter nickname (or official government name!), you have that option, too.

Listen, I love a personalized gift for yourself, but I gotta say, these totes make amazing presents for the loved ones in your life! You really can’t go wrong with something customized—it feels thoughtful, personal, and like you put in extra effort to find something special. Have a bachelorette party or wedding coming up? These would also make great goodie bags for your guests! Either way, this deal couldn’t have come at a better time with the holiday season right around the corner.

#6663. People Can’t Stop Talking About Queen Camilla Running Off With an Umbrella While King Charles Got Drenched

The weather wasn’t on King Charles’s side during his and Queen Camilla’s Caribbean tour. Charles got completely soaked during the annual Independence Ceremonial Parade at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in Antigua and Barbuda on Sunday, November 1—and the internet is losing it at his reaction.

As he attempted to celebrate 45 years of the country’s independence during the parade, Charles appeared visibly annoyed when he was left to his own devices in the rain. According to a People report, the king was “fuming” at aides who were scrambling to find him an umbrella.

People couldn’t contain their thoughts once they caught wind of the clip. One person criticized the King’s behavior, writing, “Remember when Kings went to WAR???”

Someone else chimed in, “Bit of rain is about all he ever has to worry about. Must be nice.” Others even joked that he was worried about “melting” in the wet weather.

“He’s 77 years old. It’s unacceptable to expect anyone of that age to stand in pouring rain, let alone a visiting head of state,” someone else wrote in the king’s defense. Someone else pointed out that he was likely worried about his health conditions, adding, “Very understandable as he has cancer and also is at an age where you can get pneumonia.”

That’s not all the internet had to say about the matter. In another clip circulating online, Charles continued getting soaked as Queen Camilla ran toward some shelter after she was handed her umbrella.

“I thought it was hysterical that Camilla grabbed the umbrella and ran off with it!” someone shared, while others suggested that other members of the royal family, including Meghan Markle and Charles’s late ex, Princess Diana, would have shared their umbrellas during his time of need.

Things smoothed over eventually, as Charles finally received an umbrella. He and Camilla were even photographed once they were seated away from the rain, laughing about the situation.

That being said…Charles probably relates to Barbra Streisand’s “Don’t Rain on My Parade” a little differently now.

#6662. 33 Gifts for Wives Who Hope You've Been Listening

One of the great pleasures of being married is bearing witness to your life partner's tastes and obsessions. And you'd think all that inside knowledge would make buying her a gift a cinch, and yet here you are, looking up the best gifts for wives. No judgment—we've been there. Whether it's an anniversary, a birthday, or just an occasion to remind her how much you appreciate her, we've rounded up a few things that have been on our radar all year. And yes, you should probably make that dinner reservation, too.

Still got names on your list? We've got ideas. Peruse the rest of our gift guides, and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a regular dispatch of things we think are worth your money.

It's easy to get distracted by all the excellent cashmere at Banana, but the brand knows its way around silk, too. This shirt is cut roomy and relaxed, with the sort of effortless drape that makes getting dressed easy.

Coach's Empire Carryall comes in a whole family of sizes, all cut from the brand's soft glovetanned leather. It's a beautiful bag on its own, but I'd suggest picking out a few charms to dangle from the handles to make it hers.

Phoebe Philo's Peak sunglasses are aptly named: the shape is, quite simply, peak. An absolute stunner of a pair, and just imagine her walking into brunch wearing them.

Depending on whom you ask, the Moon Shoe might just be Nike's defining sneaker of the moment. Credit Jacquemus, whose collaboration turned a relic of the brand's running history into one of fashion's most coveted shoes.

J.Crew has barn jackets on the brain this year, and its considerable efforts might just have you lusting after one yourself. I'm partial to the studded version, but there's plenty to choose from, including corduroy and faux shearling renditions.

A silk scarf is an endlessly good gift, if only because there are endless ways to wear one. Around her neck, in her hair, knotted onto a handbag, however she pleases, really.

Brooches are all over the runways right now, and might just be the easiest way to lend an outfit a little extra panache. This dangly little number from Lie Studio features carnelian stone, with a rich, brownish-red hue that feels of the moment.

A coworker Chris first put me onto Simuero, but it wasn't until a trip to Barcelona earlier this year that I got to see the Spanish jewelry label's work in person, at Bassal Store. Beautiful stuff, with an organic, slightly imperfect quality that's even better up close.

This is about as chic as it gets, as far as under-eye patches go. The silky patches promise a little firming power, and the set also includes the Le Lift hand cream as an extra treat.

Makeup, of course, is a tricky thing to gift, but a colleague of mine showed up to the office wearing this purple blush from Violette_FR, and I was immediately sold on the shade. I've had it on my running list of recommendations ever since.

Soft Services has shrunk its beloved exfoliating Buffing Bar down to miniature proportions, with four little bars in a very giftable set. A posh way to keep skin in check, and low-key great for travel.

There was plenty of oohing and aahing when a small sample of Maison Francis Kurkdjian's Oud Velvet Mood landed on my desk this year. A gorgeous oud with notes of peach, suede, and leather.

Dr. Sturm has built quite a following for her science-minded approach to skincare. This travel-friendly set brings together some of her signature formulas, all tucked into a fuzzy fleece bag.

Sidia's Braless Duo pairs a subtly scented mist and serum, a welcome salve for winter-weary skin.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

One floral and bittersweet, the other peachy and citrus-forward, these botanical aperitivi are deliciously complex without trying to taste like booze. Serve over ice or topped with soda.

Caraway isn't the first to make a coffee maker with an all-glass-and-steel brewing system, keeping hot coffee away from plastic. But it might just be the best-looking of the bunch, which counts when it's one of the first things they see in the morning.

What, your dinner parties don't involve serving salad with horn-handled, mother-of-pearl spoons? Gohar's nautilus shell-inspired salad servers are spectacularly unnecessary, which is why they make such a great gift.

Hario might be best known for its coffee gear, but the Japanese brand knows its way around matcha, too. This gift set includes a double-walled glass bowl and everything she needs to prepare a prower bowl of matcha.

Just the thing to christen that new matcha set. Kettl sources its teas directly from growers, and I'm currently taken with its Okuju matcha. Developed with a longtime partner in Uji, Japan's storied tea-growing region just outside Kyoto, it's a particularly fine powder with a delicate nuttiness and a wonderfully smooth finish.

Edie Parker's gemstoned lighter case has long been a go-to gift around these parts, but this year we've got our eye on the matching ashtray. No smoking equired—it makes a pretty fab catchall for jewelry, keys, and other little things.

I love the freaky pop-art vibes of this collaboration between Dusen Dusen and Venetian glassmaker Laguna~B. The pitcher is great on its own, but you can also spring for the set with two matching glasses.

Apple's new AirPods 5 come in two tiers, and the more giftable of the two is the version with the wireless charging case. You get longer battery life and swipe-to-adjust volume controls right on the stems.

For the record collector, U-Turn's Orbit Plus is one of the finest midrange turntables around. This version has a built-in phono preamp, so she can get straight to spinning records with a pair of powered speakers.

Taking its cues from Kodak's '70s-era 110 camera, Camp Snap offers a screen-free digital experience with an 8MP sensor, which is modest by today's standards, but entirely the point.

Nothing says great gift quite like an overengineered personal fan she'd never buy herself. Dyson's bladeless design is the clever bit, delivering a steady stream of air that's whisper-quiet.

If she's going to track her health, she might as well do it with the latest Oura Ring. The fifth-gen model is 40% smaller, with more proactive insights and personalized guidance to help her make sense of all that data.

Electric toothbrushes aren't exactly paragons of sustainable design, but Suri is doing its damnedest to change that. Its Pro 2.0 has recyclable plant-based brush heads, a repairable body, and a rechargeable battery designed to keep the whole thing out of a landfill for longer.

How could Theragun possibly improve on its already excellent mini massage gun, you ask? By adding heat, of course. The Mini Plus combines percussive massage with warming therapy to help loosen up sore muscles.

If cupping is good enough for the sporting elite, it's certainly worth a spot in her recovery routine. Wthn's kit includes eight silicone cups for a gentler take on the practice that can still help relieve muscle tension.

Wonder Valley's hinoki-scented bath products have won over a few of GQ's more relaxation-minded staffers. This set pairs a handsome bar of soap with a sachet of bath tea, which can be steeped a few times before it's finally spent.

Red-light technology is coming for sex toys, and Lelo's Mona Spectra is among the first to get in on the action. Expect to see plenty more of it in the years ahead, but there's nothing wrong with being an early adopter in this particular department.

#6661. Emmy Kasbit Lagos Spring 2027

Crowds of men and women gathered outside wearing their best Emmy Kasbit looks. The brand has amassed a cult-like following over the years and its signature akwete, a traditional Nigerian fabric, is hard to miss.

For spring 2027, founder and creative director Emmanuel Okoro, Emmy Kasbit found inspiration in an Indonesian designer with whom he worked earlier this year, drawing similarities between Akwete women and the Javanese women of Indonesia. “We’re very particular about culture and its preservation,” he said, adding that the two cultures might be very different on the surface, but are united in perseverance, community, and heritage. The overlaps motivated the collection’s blending of traditional Nigerian handwoven textiles and Asian silhouettes. Lightweight trousers inspired by a sarong and a poncho made out of two different types of akwete exemplified this fusion.

“It’s a fresh start for Emmy Kasbit,” he said. Indeed, it was the first season since the brand’s start 13 years ago that Okoro did not design with matching sets in mind. While the uniformity has historically performed well with his customers, he wanted to try something new. “The client doesn’t have to take the look as they see it on the runway if they don’t want to. They can take [individual] pieces.” Highlights included a white silk fringed dress and orange fringed blazer, as well as green tailored suits.

#6659. Prince Harry’s “Respectful” Move to Get Kate Middleton Back on His Side Could Be a Much-Needed Olive Branch

The Duke of Sussex is trying hard to win his sister-in-law over again.

It’s no secret that Prince Harry and his brother, Prince William, aren’t exactly friends right now—even though Harry has moved back to the UK with his wife, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. But Harry’s relationship with his sister-in-law, Catherine, Princess of Wales, has also come under serious strain amid the fallout.

Kate and Harry were once super close, but they’ve not been seen together publicly since King Charles’ Coronation in May 2023. However, it now sounds as though Harry wants to make amends, with a source close to the Sussexes telling The Times that Harry is “mindful” of the King’s upcoming trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) and the Prince and Princess of Wales’ expected visit to India, ensuring his own activities will not clash.

“Obviously with the King going to CHOGM and the Prince and Princess of Wales going to India, he knows about those things and he is obviously mindful of that as he’s planning his own activities as well,” the source said.

The King is currently on a nine-day tour of the Caribbean, which will culminate at CHOGM. Meanwhile, the Earthshot Prize Awards are due to take place in Mumbai this month, and Prince William is confirmed to attend, but it is not yet clear whether Kate will join him. If she does go, it would be her first appearance at the Earthshot awards since 2022, and a likely focus of attention in its own right.

The reported effort to avoid scheduling around major royal events comes after Harry’s GQ interview was published on the same day as the King’s ceremonial welcome for the Sultan of Oman, which raised some eyebrows. A Sussex spokesperson said the publication date was GQ’s decision and not Harry’s, but it sparked off a discussion around how the estranged prince can pull attention away from the working royals.

Against that backdrop, the idea that he is factoring the King and the Waleses’ plans into his schedule could be read as a deliberate olive branch, giving off the vibe that Harry is trying to make space for his family, rather than compete with them for headlines.

As for how Kate in particular features here, it’s reported that she was one of the go-betweens trying to keep the brothers close. In William & Catherine, royal editor Russell Myers wrote (per Marie Claire), “Whether counseling William or having a quiet word in Harry’s ear, she saw it as her duty to keep the two brothers on the same team, as did their senior aides.”

Kate has also carved out a place in the royal calendar with her annual Together at Christmas carol concert, which brings together big names and people doing good in their communities. It’s one of the moments when the spotlight is firmly on her—so Harry reportedly keeping the Waleses’ plans in mind could be an especially meaningful gesture.

#6656. Lisa Folawiyo Lagos Spring 2027

The Lagos fashion crowd loves to be entertained. Throughout the week, designers have found interesting ways to showcase their collections, from celebrities walking the runway to live dance performances. Closing out the program this season was the star Nigerian designer Lisa Folawiyo, who returned to the schedule after several years away (she last showed on schedule in 2019). To mark the occasion, she invited guests for a candle-lit dinner and a unique fashion show experience at White Space, a gallery-turned-creative studio.

Mirrored tables filled the room, each decorated with handwoven flowers, which brought a welcome touch of craft to the proceedings. Shortly after the first course, the lights dimmed, orchestral pop music queued up, and a handful of models wearing Folawiyo’s latest collection walked down the makeshift runway; this pattern repeated over three additional courses. Standout looks included a fully beaded patchwork dress with feather detailing, a black embellished lace dress, and a raffia zebra set.

The collection, titled After Rain, was designed with Africa’s tropical countries, which do not experience the four seasons, in mind. For years, many local designers have tried to fit into the seasonal calendar that brands adhere to in the West. This collection was a rebuttal to that system. Nigeria typically has only two seasons: one rainy and one not. “The main objective was to coin our season,” she said during an interview in her studio, where artisans were hand-beading the new collection. “Everything after the rain is color, sunshine, and that’s really who we are as a brand.”

The collection marked Folawiyo’s first foray into animal prints (snake, leopard, and zebra prints all featured). At first glance, several pieces looked like knitwear. A closer inspection revealed that they were made from strands of raffia dyed and intricately woven together. After some 20 years in business, Folawiyo once again reminded us of her creative prowess.

#6653. 4 Epic New Watches Every Watch Guy Is Salivating Over Right Now

Welcome to Watch Guy Watches, GQ’s monthly curation of high-end timepieces for the true watch nerds among us. This month, Moser goes retro(grade); Lange brings back a beloved bracelet; Biver drops its first hand-wound three-hander; and Breitling puts a pair of vintage-inspired watches in its core catalog.

There are only a few firm absolutes in the horological sphere. One of them is “never bet against H. Moser & Cie.” The high-end independent maker never ceases to amaze with its creativity, wit, and technological prowess. From a mechanical timepiece that bears a suspicious resemblance to a certain famous smartwatch to one the coolest integrated bracelet-bearing luxury sports watches on the market, Moser consistently delivers the Swiss-made goods.

Building upon its Pioneer Retrograde Seconds Midnight Blue release from two years ago, three new models with retrograde seconds join the collection this month in the Pioneer, Endeavour, and Streamliner collections. While all three are beautiful, however, it’s the latter whose aesthetics pair particularly well with this steampunk-esque complication—one in which a small hand tracks the passing seconds in an arc and then jumps back to its starting position at the top of each 30-second period.

Housed in a 40mm brushed stainless steel cushion case with a serpentine integrated bracelet, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds offers a potent mix of Streamline Moderne and futurism before one even considers its dial. Executed in midnight blue fumé enamel, it features applied indices and the brand’s signature modified syringe handset, with a faint “H. Moser & Cie” signature appearing in white beneath 12 o’clock. The lower half of the face, meanwhile, is given over to the retrograde seconds display. Inspired by instrument gauges such as automotive speedometers, it features smooth action powered by the cal. HMC 252, a product of movement specialists Agenhor. (Flip the watch over and you can view its tungsten rotor whirring away via a sapphire caseback.)

One of the coolest features of the Streamliner collection is that despite the presence of numerous complications; of the use of fumé dials; and of high-end pricing, these watches are meant to be used. With 120m of water resistance, steel constriction, automatic winding, and 72 hours of power reserve, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds is effectively a high-end tool watch. (Though at a sticker price of 29,900 CHF, maybe take it off if you’re, like, climbing Mt. Everest or whatever?)

While retrograde seconds displays don’t have the same utility as calendar readouts or GMT complications, they do demonstrate horological competence on the part of the watchmaker…and more importantly, they’re wild fun to watch in action. And if you can’t have a little fun in your watch-collecting journey, well—then what the heck are you even doing here, anyway?!

If you’ve been waiting years for the return of platinum bracelet options for A. Lange & Söhne’s Datograph Perpetual watch, we give you permission to rejoice: a new version of the timepiece—made in honor of the model’s 20th anniversary—is equipped not only with a diamond-studded black dial, but with a fresh matching platinum bracelet. Designed with five links rather than the seven of early-2000s models made by German jewelry manufacturer Wellendorff, said bracelet is perhaps more notable than the watch itself, which features the brand’s manually wound manufacture Calibre L952.1 movement and is limited to just 50 pieces.

When watch-world elder statesman Jean-Cladue Biver and his son Pierre co-founded their eponymous firm in 2022, their introductory product was a half-million-dollar automatic tourbillon and minute repeater. Having since added a simple automatic three-hander to their lineup in the form of the Automatique, they’re now expanding their offerings with a hand-wound three-hander in stainless steel. Dubbed the AB, it measures 38mm wide and 9.8mm tall and features a beautiful black multi-level onyx dial with gold accents, plus a cool stainless steel bracelet with an angular five-link design and a patented micro-adjust system. Powered by the new Calibre JCB-004 designed in collaboration with Le Cercle des Horlogers, it’s the brand’s entry-level model…though it’ll still set you back roughly the cost of a BMW M3. (Naturally, it’s already sold out.)

On the slightly less eye-watering—but no less compelling—end of the watch-guy spectrum is the new Breitling Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41. Why does it look so familiar, you might ask? Effectively, it’s a modern version of the famed ref. 806 “Twin Jet”-logo chronograph from the 1960s, only this time, it’s available as a non-limited edition—a fact that will surely excite deep Breitling aficionados. Measuring 41mm in stainless steel, it’s manually wound just like its vintage namesake, and comes paired to a brown leather strap for $7,900 or to a handsome steel bracelet for $8,400. If you fancy something a bit more left-field, there’s also a hand-wound, non-limited version of the Cosmonaute, a riff on the Navitimer equipped with a 24-hour dial that was famously worn by astronaut Scott Carpenter in 1962 ($10,600-$11,000).

#6652. Want to Take Your Voting Plan from Drab to Fab? Tack On A Little Treat

I’ll be the first to say that voting in American elections is both an increasingly urgent civic duty and, let’s face it, a bit of a drag sometimes. Still, I haven’t missed my chance to vote since I turned 18 (no small feat for a chronic procrastinator with ADHD). My secret? Tacking on something more fun—an embarrassingly over-sweetened seasonal latte at my college coffee shop in Ohio, a mani-pedi at my favorite queer salon in Austin, a shopping trip at Wasteland in Los Angeles—to help get me out the door.

My plan for this year’s midterms has been set in stone for weeks. First, I’ll cast my ballot at the Los Angeles LGBT Center—a wonderful community resource for harm-reduction supplies like Narcan and test strips, as well as theater and breakfast burritos. Then I’ll take the bus to LACMA to check out the new David Geffen Galleries and repair to my favorite Ethiopian spot afterward for injera and a glass of tej.

Would I vote in the midterms even if I couldn’t do anything cute after? Of course. But given the overall grimness of the current political climate, I’m snatching pockets of joy where I can—especially if they’re accessible by public transit.

As it turns out, I’m not the only one attaching a little side quest to my voting plan. Sophie, 35, threw a voting party so that she and her friends could fill out their Oregon mail-in ballots together, with her husband dishing out homemade curry and, she says, making “a silly PowerPoint about different issues on the ballot.” Hannah, 39, is going to bring her young child to her polling place and possibly host a party of her own.

For Nina, 26, voting in person has always been “a task I sometimes come close to forgetting, even though I desperately care about our country’s political future.” So she’s resolved to take advantage of the fact that her New York polling place is near Tiny Doll House—arguably the city’s best miniatures store—and buy herself the mini chaise lounge she’s been eyeing after she casts her vote. James, 19, who is voting in New York’s midterm elections for the very first time this year, wants to mark the occasion with a showing of Wicker at Cobble Hill Cinemas, followed by dinner at Sam’s Italian Cuisine on Court Street.

Given the ongoing issue of low voter turnout in key states, I think we could stand to make voting a little more engaging—and thanks to my long-held “vote + something fun” ritual, I now associate that privilege with the quick dopamine hit of little-treat culture. Sure, it would be great if all Americans were champing at the bit to exercise their voting rights, reward or not—but if getting your favorite sandwich before you cast your ballot or seeing a movie afterward gets you to the polls …why not?

Some internet sleuths may have cracked the code on tonight’s performance lineup after zooming in on a mirror selfie posted to DWTS troupe member Kamri Peterson’s Instagram Stories on Monday, November 2.

According to the pic, DWTS’s Disney Night performance lineup is as follows:

On top of each celeb’s individual dances with their pro partners, tonight marks the first time groups will be divided for team dances. After Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold close off the regular dances, the team dances will commence.

Team Slaytopia—comprised of Alfonso Ribeiro, Tatyana Ali, Jan Ravnik, Maura Higgins, Mark Ballas, Amber Glenn, Pasha Pashkov, Julia Stiles, and Ezra Sosa—will take the ballroom stage first. Then, Team Wildcats—Julianne Hough, Ezra Frech, Dani Karagach, Jenna Dewan, Val Chmerkovskiy, Harry Shum Jr., Jenna Johnson, Connor, and Rylee—will follow with their group number.

He added, “There’s strategy involved with who they put at the top of the show and who they’re putting at the very top of that next hour and who they’re putting at the end as well.”

#6650. Samira Nasr’s November Editor’s Letter: On Performance

From Natalie Portman to the dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White, this month’s issue is all about those whose art takes place in front of an audience

I’m writing this from Paris as the Spring 2027 shows are wrapping up. One glorious night, I had the chance to see Céline Dion during her residency at the Plénitude Arena. What really struck me about her performance was her unique ability to unite an entire stadium. It was just her up there—no background dancers—using her voice to bring us along on her journey. It was deeply moving. I was reminded of how vital performance can be. I’m sure there were people in the arena whose lives and experiences and politics differ from my own, but we could all come together to revel in the sheer joy of an incredible show.

That is the spirit in which we celebrate this issue’s theme, performance. A performer can entertain us, transport us, and, crucially, connect us.

Our cover star, Natalie Portman, photographed by Carlijn Jacobs and styled by our style director at large, Malina Joseph Gilchrist, has consistently transported us over the years with great performances. In the coming months, she will deliver two more, in Cathy Yan’s biting art-world satire, The Gallerist, and in Lena Dunham’s hyped new rom-com, Good Sex. Both reveal a lighter, more humorous, though by no means less committed side of Portman, and that’s by design. “Right now,” she tells our executive editor, Leah Chernikoff, she’s focusing on “a lot of joy. I think it’s both for myself and what I hope to offer an audience. There’s a lot of really heavy stuff going on … and so it does feel like the biggest service you can do right now as an artist is to deliver some joy.”

Elsewhere in this issue, I am thrilled to feature a range of dancers, musicians, writers, and actors whose work I have long revered. The dream team of John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White came together in conversation to discuss their new stage adaptation of the classic American novel and film Imitation of Life, which also marks Legend’s first musical. “At the core, this is a story about the American dream, with all of its contradictions and complications,” says Nottage.

Sarah Hoover brings us the story of one of ballet’s great modern partnerships—American Ballet Theatre’s Isabella Boylston and James Whiteside—as they prepare to dance their final performances together. Boylston, who welcomed her first child this summer, returned to the barre six weeks after giving birth in order to be ready to partner with Whiteside before he retires next summer. “If I had to go onstage with him tonight in Swan Lake, with zero rehearsal, I’d still feel good about it,” Boylston tells Hoover.

When this issue is on newsstands, our podcast, The Good Buy, cohosted by Chernikoff and our executive digital director, Lynette Nylander, will be back for its fourth season, available wherever you get your podcasts and on YouTube, featuring another incredible lineup of folks whose style we’re obsessed with, including Paloma Elsesser and Kim Kardashian. Each episode is a reminder that getting dressed is the ultimate performance.

Opening image: Celine cape and dress. Tiffany & Co. Bird on a Rock by Tiffany Wings earrings.

She’s found her new favorite statement hue

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Jennifer Lawrence’s street style may gravitate toward the minimal, but she’s a strong advocate when it comes to the unexpected pop of color. Sure, she loves her branded baseball caps and her chunky pendants, but her most common trick has become incorporating a vibrant statement piece (or two), whether it’s a pair of baby-pink party pants, a lime-green handbag, or some blood-red mesh flats.

This fall, Lawrence is at again as she eschews the standard autumnal palette for her new favorite color: chartreuse.

Just a few weeks ago, the Oscar winner turned heads when she stepped out in a yellow-green Miu Miu cardigan, and now, it appears she’s doubling down on her chartreuse campaign.

On Wednesday, Lawrence was seen walking around New York City in that same electric cardigan, layered underneath a matching cotton overcoat from rising NYC-based designer and LVMH Prize finalist Colleen Allen. (Upon a closer look, you could see that she even wore a scrunchie in the same color, too.)

If anyone can pull off stacks of chartreuse though, it’s Lawrence, and she balanced the eye-popping pieces with a few grounding base layers, including a white graphic tee and some black slacks. She also added inky calf-hair loafers from the Row, a set of oversize sunglasses from Dita Eyewear, and a handwoven tote from Tory Burch.

These past few years, we’ve seen the domination of everything from butter yellow to “brat” green. Now, it seems Lawrence is making the case for a neon tint somewhere right down the middle.

#6646. Designer Susan Alexandra Made Her Dream Butter Yellow Gown for Her Wedding at a Historic French Villa

Susan Alexandra Korn and Andy Nahman officially met in March 2023 at writer Naomi Fry’s birthday party in Brooklyn. But as it happens, Susan actually caught Andy’s eye more than a year earlier, when he attended the October 2021 opening of her Lower East Side store featuring her namesake jewelry and accessories.

“I walked into this magical polychromatic dream world, well over capacity, with her family, friends, colleagues, and collaborators,” says Andy, who was invited to the party by his sister, writer and editor Haley Nahman. “Susan’s energy was palpable, not only because it was like standing inside her mind’s eye, but in the community surrounding her. I remember going home feeling in awe of her magnetic energy and vision.” But it was at that birthday party, held at artist Al Freeman’s home, where they really “clicked,” says Susan.

Andy proposed to Susan in September 2025, on a trip to the South of France. He had a plan: “Take a short drive from our hotel to the Matisse chapel, surprise Susan with my proposal, and subsequently toast to our future with some bubbles,” says Andy, who is a VP of data science at Disney. But when they arrived at the chapel, it was closed—and the fluted glasses had broken in the car trunk. “Andy improvised quickly,” Susan says, “and proposed on the curb outside of the chapel as a few people looked on quizzically from a bus stop.”

The mishap only made it all the more special. “I think we will equally remember my kneeling proposal alongside the scene in the trunk: exploded flowers, broken flutes, and rapidly melting ice. Luckily, the bottle was still intact and we opened it,” Andy says.

Susan and Andy were married on August 29 at Villa Magnan in Biarritz, France. They chose the historic venue because, as Susan says, “it’s dripping with rustic charm and special touches. Hector the Donkey ambling around the lawn while two elder dogs lazily bark from their sun spots. It’s beautiful and old but very inviting.”

From the beginning, when envisioning the celebration, Susan—who is known for her candy-colored creations—zeroed in on the floral design. “I am obsessive about flowers and about only using flowers in season,” she says. She envisioned a “cake of flowers”—a living sculpture of sorts. The family who owns the villa pulled it off, along with a flower-covered chuppah for the ceremony. In addition to the villa’s in-house team, Susan and Andy worked with event producers Mathilde and Ann Charlotte of Sauce to bring it all together.

Festivities began on Friday, when they had their guests board a “petit train to a secret location,” says Susan. “The train zigzagged through Biarritz and dropped us at the lighthouse. We drank Champagne as the sun dipped into the ocean.” From there, they took buses to the nearby town of Saint-Jean-de-Luz, where they rented out a restaurant called Denen Kanttua for a welcome dinner of classic Basque cuisine: pâté, eggs with roe, tuna crudo, mussels, financiers, and lots of wine.

The cherry on top? “We commissioned a local artisan to sculpt our Chihuahua, Pigeon, out of French salted butter,” Susan says. “He was delicious, served with radishes and hunks of bread.”

For the Friday night event, Susan wore a nude tulle and paillette-embellished dress by Jenny Packham, sourced from Vinted. “Everyone asked if I designed the dress because it was so quintessentially me,” Susan says. She paired it with vintage Beverly Feldman Lucite heels. Andy wore a natural linen suit and shirt from Stoffa and chocolate suede loafers from Morjas.

As a designer, Susan always knew she would make her own wedding dress. She worked with her director of production to bring it to life. “Over the course of six months, Melissa and I worked with a patternmaker, a couturier, and master of embellishments to create ‘The Dress’ and the after-party gown.”

For her ceremony, Susan designed a gown made of a soft butter yellow duchesse satin. “The silhouette was based on a gown from the 1930s. We gussied up the dress with rhinestone flowers and cherubs holding roses. The cherubs represented Andy and me, and the roses represented our ever-growing love,” she says. She accessorized with a pair of Art Deco–inspired pearl drop and enamel pansy earrings of her own design, a borrowed diamond tennis necklace, and golden Manolo Blahnik kitten heels from The Real Real. She also carried a floral sequined purse with her and Andy’s names embroidered in pink on the inside.

Andy wore a custom suit from Saman Amel in a deep earthy brown with a RRL shirt and a vintage Hermès tie emblazoned with tiny carrots and radishes that Susan gave him for his birthday, plus loafers from Our Legacy. Susan’s after-party dress was custom-made by the artisans who make Susan Alexandra jewelry and bags. It was “a sequined manifestation of the future I want,” Susan says. “It featured a house surrounded by an abundant garden and Pigeon embroidered on the tush.”

Alison Roman, who is a close friend of the couple, officiated the ceremony. They walked down the villa staircase to a gentle live piano rendition of “Avril 14th” by Aphex Twin. “The incredible power that is Alison Roman married us under the chuppah,” Susan says. “She read a heartfelt speech about observing Andy and me in our natural states, coexisting in harmony, holding different parts of the coin of life. Alison said that in marriage, the colors grow deeper and richer with time. It was so tender and so loving. It is a special person who can officiate a wedding with such ease and grace, and she is that special person,” says Susan.

In Andy’s vows, “he promised to never let me go too long without flowers and to always fill my cup, both with coffee and love,” Susan says. “Both our vows had so much overlap, so much hope for our future and so much love. Many mentions of Pigeon were made, which made me cry,” she adds.

“I am not drawn to public speaking and had anticipated nerves around sharing our vows,” Andy adds, reflecting on the ceremony. “What I learned is that it is extremely comfortable to speak publicly when what you are saying is your truth from the heart.”

For dessert, the newlyweds decided on a “pavlova the size of a small country,” Susan shares. “Every guest grabbed a spoon, and we dug in and ate it communally, leaving plates untouched.” Susan’s sister, Janie Korn, made them a custom cake topper of miniature versions of themselves.

After dinner and dessert, the couple and their guests danced to a set by DJ Alex Chapman, followed by a special impromptu DJ set by Jason Stewart (a.k.a. Them Jeans), who was a guest at the wedding. “We danced, drank, ate sandwiches, and talked until the moon began to set,” Susan says.

We asked guests to meet at Le Grande Plage for a surprise. We boarded le petit train, which zigzagged through beautiful Biarritz.

The trolley brought us to the Biarritz Lighthouse! We sipped Champagne as the sun dipped into the sea. Magnifique!

A sweet stolen moment. I suspect we are out of body here.

We orchestrated many (delightful) twists and turns throughout the evening. Here, our guests are being ushered into buses for the next surprise.

A reenactment of the final scene of The Graduate, but less forlorn.

The joyful gaze as we jet off to our next locale!

Making our Chihuahua, Pigeon, into a demi-sel beurre sculpture was Andy’s brainchild. It was adorned with hunks of bread and radishes, and I’ve never had a more delicious dog. The mini butter cake is that same divine French butter infused with Espelette pepper, which is unique to Basque country. Created by Bonjour Gateau.

Wedding guests shmoozing outside of the restaurant Denen Kanttua. We were in a charming Basque town, Saint-Jean-de-Luz. Another person who married here: King Louis XIV.

Welcoming everyone to the wedding and sharing how surreal this moment was.

Hugging all these beautiful people from my life and Andy’s life and now…our life?

My sister, Janie (with her husband, Punit), gave a delightful toast. She declared, “If I’m going to be under anyone’s thumb in this life, I’m glad it’s Susan’s.” I’m not sure she will ever forgive me for making her speak in public.

Andy’s dad, Vance, bestowing final touches to the groom.

My friend Kim’s Nightshade bag, lounging with my veil. Spoiler: The bag did not make it back to NYC in one piece.

Doria insisted on a veil. (“When else in your life will you wear a veil?!”) So here I am, veiled.

Weddings feel like a portal to another time. As I was designing my wedding ensembles, I thought of black-and-white photos of ancestors in gilded frames. With this in mind, we created an Edwardian-style veil worn low on the head. Satin rosettes with beaded stamens secured the veil in my hair.

I spotted a dark aubergine calla lily in the bouquet and had to yank it out right before this picture was taken. It was disrupting the harmony of the other bright flowers.

The Dress was inspired by 1930s Hollywood sirens and the sun—two things I worship. I sketched floating flowers and cherubs, and the artisans re-created the drawings with rhinestones.

The veil was made from a yard of fabric I found balled up in an antiques shop in Connecticut. I asked the store owner about the origin of the fabric: “It’s 60 years old, from a now-closed boutique on Madison Avenue.” I have a shop on Madison Avenue and thought it was beshert.

Dear friends who showed up in my room as I was getting ready. I felt so loved and supported. Women are so magnificent. From left: Sarah, Rachel, Lisa, Kim, me, Sierra, Doria, and Alison. Aren’t they lovely?

A statuesque Andy, awaiting his grand entrance.

Reciting my vows, flanked by oleander bushes. I assume this is where I was telling Andy that I promise to always harmonize on improvised songs about Pigeon.

No one tells you how delightful vows are. It’s just standing and listening to someone wax poetic about you.

Our dear, special friend Alison Roman officiated the wedding. She made such a beautiful speech about how the colors of marriage deepen as time passes. She is so soulful and was with me the night Andy and I met. Here I am asking her if it’s okay if we kiss. She was like, “Do whatever you want!”

What a surreal moment. We had just left the altar and were suspended in this unbelievable moment of disbelief, joy, and love.

Andy and flowers: two things I deeply love.

Me and my new family members: Avi, Haley, Andy, Matt, Kelly, Kathy, Vance.

A sister pic! Andy and I are so lucky to have sisters. From left: Kelly, Andy, me, Haley (little Dove is in there!), and Janie.

From left: Adam, Mom, Andy, me, Rick, and Janie.

Weddings are not known for great food, and we wanted ours to be the exception. The food at our wedding was a priority. The restaurant at Villa Magnan is extraordinary; every bite was divine. This is a platter of Sucrine lettuce, smoked anchovies, raw cream, and wild herbs.

Every single touch at Villa Magnan was considered. They scattered big dahlias everywhere the eye lands.

The custom sequined bag was perfectly attuned to my gown. Our wedding dates and names are embroidered in the lining of the bag, a surprise touch from the artisan.

This greenhouse-cum-kitchen is where all of the beautiful food was made (with love).

Perfect in situ at Villa Magnan. A bundle of Espelette peppers, dried flowers from the garden, a hand-painted fruit mirror, and strings of beads.

Did we purposely align our wedding with tomato season in France? Perhaps.

My friend Lisa handmade the place cards using seashells and a healthy smattering of googly eyes. The shells were a nod to our seaside locale. Every setting was adorned with a different beaded charm: an Espelette pepper, a pigeon (for our dog), or a donkey (Hector is the resident donkey at Villa Magnan). I illustrated the menus and Andy developed a custom font.

Janie made custom ceramic vases for my wedding and, in an act of extreme love and devotion, shlepped them from London. It was no small feat. Her work made the tables majestic.

Janie’s seashell creature place card was among my favorites.

A glowing moment before the food was served.

Listening to my friend Brian give the speech of a lifetime.

Everyone said such wonderful things. It’s like, “Wow, people actually love us?” Tears were shed.

Danny’s speech was so soulful, so wise, so tender. Every woman asked for his number afterward. You see, a well-delivered wedding speech is the ultimate dating app.

My pops, David. His speech integrated all the French words he knows, c/o Pepé Le Pew, Amélie, and the Madeline books.

After dinner, Andy and I slunk back to our room, where I changed for the after-party. I made this sequined dress, which was a manifestation of our future: a cottage with a garden, flowers, and butterflies. On the back was a bedazzled Pigeon.

I did my own hair and makeup and got ready in 45 minutes. I’ve been doing my hair and makeup for 100 years, so I figured I may as well do it on this day. Looking back, I’m really impressed I was able to adhere false lashes for the first time ever on my wedding day.

Some of the favorite moments from the wedding were the short bottle episodes where Andy and I were alone together. Back in our room, drinking Champagne, the party is on the horizon.

Janie made us hand-sculpted custom cake toppers! Nothing is more special. I will cherish them forever.

Our cake toppers look on with glee and perhaps pride.

The wedding cake was sublime: Vanilla bean gateau was layered with caramelized praline paste. We scattered raspberries on top as guests cheered. The cake wore a skirt of meringue puffs and, as a final touch, a dusting of powdered sugar by Andy.

A shower of sugar as “Chapel of Love” played.

Michelle and Karolyn are two people who make every event a party.

My dear friend the illustrious Alex Chapman, DJ’d the first part of the night, followed by a special Them Jeans set. A highlight of the evening was Jason playing (the song of the summer) “Pink Blush” by Dolly Babe.

Dancing with my mama and Andy. No better feeling!

My former Chicago crew, Lisa and Alex. We became adults together and now, here we are, elder adults. Aww.

See my above note about Michelle. Steph is also joyful, glowing.

All I ever wanted for the night: color, love, joy.

#6645. 7 Celebrity Outfits You Should Steal This Month

With the holidays looming and next year’s awards season on the horizon, there’s no rest for the A-list weary. Between hitting up screenings, press junkets, and the general business of being a star, you’ll occasionally catch famous folks kicking their feet up in suites at SoFi Stadium or risking a courtside collision with a referee at an NBA game.

From Harry Styles getting his heart rate up on morning runs over the Williamsburg Bridge to Ethan Hawke turning up for a SAG screening, Glenn Close pulling an absolute grail piece from a film she starred in alongside Robert Redford, and Nicholas Hoult hopping between planes, the celebrity style circuit is showing no signs of slowing down.

Maybe this is the season you’ve been influenced to go all in on corduroy, resurrect those vintage graphic tees gathering dust in your tote bins, or finally dip your dainty toes into the jazz shoe craze. Whatever your sartorial itch, let these celebrities do the legwork for you.

The Hawkester has worn corduroy before, and this look calls to mind Robin Williams in Dead Poets Society, whose affinity for the fabric felt like part of the curriculum. Hawke styles the suit in a way that feels less adjunct professor and more stoner student, thanks to a ratty graphic tee and tinted shades. Rather than dress shoes, he opts for well-worn dark brown Sambas, which contrast nicely with his acorn-colored suit. Carpe diem, and all that.

The star of Netflix’s upcoming show The Altruists demonstrates how dressing in a flowy, monochromatic palette doesn’t have to feel boring. The burgundy trench coat injects just enough color to keep things interesting. Leave it open so you don’t look like Inspector Gadget, and throw on tinted sunglasses, because they’re never a bad idea, no matter the fit.

With his Together, Together tour wrapping up at the end of the month, Harry’s New York stroll fits will likely be inducted into the annals of celeb big fits. He seems to have tapped into the lore of ’90s-era skaters, layering a long-sleeved tee under a T-shirt. Add light-wash jeans, all-white sneakers, and Apple earbuds, and you’ve got a man who feels gloriously analog in a digital world.

Glenn Close shows us how to build an outfit around a statement piece, in this case, a jacket from The Natural, the 1984 film in which she co-starred. Throw on navy slacks, loafers, and a crisp white Oxford shirt, and you’re good to go. Of course, it helps when you have iconic films attached to your name, too.

Example 1,088 of why denim-on-denim is always the answer to the in-flight outfit dilemma. Mr. Hoult opts for a charcoal-hued Canadian tuxedo, offset by black boots and a dad cap. Denim can take a beating. Whether from turbulence-induced coffee spills or an overenthusiastic recline, it provides a welcome layer of warmth on those cold and bone-dry flights.

As the oldest brother in Sweden’s Skarsgård acting dynasty, Alexander proves that an age-old graphic tee and Chuck Taylors will always be a can’t-miss combination.
