#6643. Do You Need a Night Cream? The 10 Best Picks for Dryness, Sensitive Skin, Fine Lines, and More

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Sleep may be free, but great skin takes a little investment. So while you're dreaming about running away to Tuscany or that boy you matched with on Hinge (guilty), your face is quietly clocking in for the night shift. Its objectives? Repairing and renewing with the help of the right night cream—because the right one can turn those eight hours of unconsciousness into a full-blown glow-up, coaxing out collagen and smoothing the fine lines that betray our Netflix habits.

Of course, you could just use a moisturizer, but a night cream is richer, often filled with firming and plumping ingredients that work best overnight. Not sure which is for you? Fear not, because there's a night cream out there for everyone, whether you've got dry skin, wrinkles, dark spots, or anything in between. To help you find your perfect match, I’ve rounded up the best night creams for all skin types and concerns. So, consider the following your skin's version of a silk pillowcase: indulgent, effective, and worth every last dreamy drop.

“This is a heaven-sent nourishing moisturizer for sensitive, dry, and acne-prone skin. My aesthetician, Madalaina Conti, first recommended this for me. I love it not only for acne, but it helps with my tight, flaky skin that I get in the winter months. When I use this overnight, it brings back all the plumpness and hydration. When I’m really dry, I’ll put on a thick layer like a mask and sleep in it.”—JASMINE HYMAN, ASSISTANT BEAUTY EDITOR

“I understand the purpose of a night cream is to be thick and cocoon-like on your face. But when you want all the moisture without your face sticking to your pillow, this ‘cloud cream’ from Kiehl’s is perfect. It’s got a whipped texture that feels really light, yet it’s packed with squalane, rich lipids, and shea butter.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

“The fine lines around my eyes look less noticeable, and my under-eyes suddenly seems like I’m getting sleep again. I’m 29 and starting to think about taking extra care of my eyes and neck, so I’ve been focusing on those two areas every night for the last two months. And I really notice a difference. My eyes look brighter and more awake in the morning, and my under-eye bags aren’t as prominent.”—BG

“If you have super dry skin and suffer from redness and irritation, this is the night cream for you. The thick consistency is deeply moisturising, cocooning your skin in a rich, soothing layer. The formula itself is infused with Japanese indigo and ceramides, which help to calm irritation, strengthen your skin barrier, and leave you waking up looking like you actually got eight hours of sleep (even if you didn't).”—LIA MAPPOURA, BEAUTY WRITER

“I’ve used up a few tubs of this ultra-rich moisturizer. It’s my go-to in the winter when my skin gets quite dry. It feels so luxe, even down to the glass jar, but is a mere fraction of the price of so many of my other favorites (and I love that I can pick it up quickly from the drugstore whenever I need it).”—BG

“If you're a loyal retinol user, listen up because Medik8's Advanced Night Restore was made with you in mind. This rich yet fast-absorbing cream is designed to be applied after your retinoid, helping to soothe, strengthen, and deeply nourish skin overnight. Infused with ceramides, antioxidants, and a reparative peptide complex, it reinforces the skin's barrier and locks in moisture, making it ideal for dry, sensitive complexions.”—LM

“I randomly started using this when I was very young and had not a single wrinkle on my face. But I loved the rich texture so much; it made my skin look so glowy and fresh. I felt like I woke up with better skin every time I used it. Now at 29, I’m returning back to it, and I realize this is so freakin’ good to add into any anti-aging routine. This cream is loaded with moisturizing ingredients, which is a must if you’re trying to offset dryness from any actives like retinol or AHAs.”—BG

“As a beauty writer, I'm often asked what my favorite skincare brand is. And while I experiment with many daily, my response always remains the same. Cetaphil! The dermatologist-recommended brand is a failsafe option for me, not only for its pared-back formulas that work twice as hard as the fancy brands (and don't irritate my sensitive, breakout-prone skin), but also for its price. I mean, you can't go wrong with a product that’s less than $15. The Rich Night Cream is just that: rich in consistency to hydrate yet not overbear the skin. Breathable yet effective, if you will.”—LM

A night cream is any cream that you use at night before bed to hydrate your skin. The idea is that night creams are thicker and made with rich emollients that work well to seal in hydration overnight versus your standard moisturizer that could be applied day or night. But a night cream can be a cream for nighttime, even if it’s not explicitly called a night cream. FWIW, that’s more of a marketing term than anything.

You absolutely need a moisturizer before bed, even if you have oily skin. But do you need a specific cream that’s called a “night cream”? Not necessarily, so long as your nighttime moisturizer is doing its job of hydrating and locking in moisture while you sleep.

How to choose the right night cream for you

If you have dry skin, the night cream selection process will probably be a breeze for you. Most night creams contain a plethora of ingredients to moisturize your skin. But some of those can be too heavy for oily and/or acne-prone skin. If you want something on the lighter side, avoid anything with a lot of butters and oils, like shea butter or cocoa butter. Lightweight hydrators include squalane, jojoba oil, hyaluronic acid, and panthenol.

Look for a mix of hydrators and sealants.

The key to moisturizing your skin is two-fold: Hydrate, then lock in moisture. Hydration comes from humectants, aka ingredients that pull water into your skin. That’s glycerin, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, and aloe vera. But once you’ve hydrated, you want to keep all that water in your skin, which is where sealants come in. That’s oils and butters. They create a barrier over your skin to keep moisture from seeping out. Together, the two create a formula that offers lasting hydration, not just a quit hit of plumpness.

#6641. Sinéad O'Dwyer Spring 2027 Ready-to-Wear

The body in motion has long fascinated Sinéad O’Dwyer. For spring 2027, a central piece was a shimmering sequin-covered slip dress onto which blurred photographs of bodies in the throes of performance were transposed. The photos, lensed by Ottilie Landmark, originated from Knead, a movement piece O’Dwyer developed with choreographer Grace Nicol at London’s Barbican Centre in 2025, which explored the dynamics of watching and being watched, and the desire to be seen. The influence of that dance performance could be felt throughout Notice Me, a collection concerned with how clothes cultivate, capitulate to, or coalesce with bodily brilliance.

First presented in the Victoria and Albert Museum’s Raphael Court, and subsequently captured in an intimate lookbook by Landmark, the collection traced an ongoing shift in O’Dwyer’s approach to making clothes. “There’s a lot of newness, but I suppose for me it’s in a direction of making things a bit more easy to buy and wear,” she explained. O’Dwyer’s practice is built around richly technical, body-inclusive construction; here, she refined her methods rather than relinquished them.

A dance of spectacle and practicality played out most in tailoring, a growing category for O’Dwyer. A double-breasted jacket with a masculine silhouette featured a sensual inward curve at the waist, while zippered jackets and corset tops, paired with matching trousers and hip-skimming pencil skirts, amplified the utilitarian approach. O’Dwyer developed the tailoring by padding out the back and seat of a mannequin, using that exaggerated curvature to inform the cut of jackets and shirting that retained their masculine, oversized proportions.

Meanwhile, pourable sequin dresses with sweat-like surfaces were constructed on stretch mesh, and satin-y, icy blue and green slip dresses and other fine knit gowns moved freely while retaining sculptural shapes. Sporty stretch fabrics were put to work on pale dresses and separates, with softly gathered bustlines and shapes that caressed rather than encased. The pattern cutting, O’Dwyer explained, was intended to accommodate a wider range of proportions without relying on fixed cup sizes or extensive alterations. The aforementioned zippers allow wearers to adjust fit and exposure. Micro-shorts with doubled waistbands introduced a more athletic note. Clothes with a certain toughness were offset by the delicate details of lingerie, and even sheer mesh bralettes were adorned with tiny satin buttons and long, trailing ribbons.

Those buttons were among the collection’s most labor-intensive achievements. O’Dwyer has been developing an embroidery technique in which they are chain-stitched into the garment as it is constructed, with approximately 4,000 featuring on each of two intricate long-sleeved gowns. Such pieces now belong firmly to the designer’s bespoke and made-to-order offering, rather than ready-to-wear. It is a pragmatic distinction for a house where occasionwear is becoming an increasingly important part of the business.

This was a season that built upon a new brand identity, including an updated logo, and reflected the designer’s awareness that the customers who have worn her label since its beginnings have grown up, too. The collection will be sold exclusively through her own e-commerce platform, giving O’Dwyer greater control over pricing and the pace of its release. Rather than abandoning the craftsmanship that has distinguished her work, she is finding more appropriate homes for her techniques, while making the rest of the wardrobe more accessible. O’Dwyer’s allegiance to the ever-amorphous body remains as insistent as ever, but spring 2027 suggested that accommodating its realities can be every bit as compelling as showcasing them.

#6638. Meg Stalter Plays the Ultimate Holiday Diva for Marc Jacobs

Hop into Marc Jacobs’ “Let It Joy” campaign, a snowed-in, holiday ride with bags, beauty, and gifts galore.

The new Marc Jacobs holiday campaign had me thinking of that famous Sex and the City image: Carrie charging out into a snowstorm in a fabulous fur coat, heels, and a sequin beanie, off to spend the holidays with Miranda. Now, picture Meg Stalter in her own fur coat and matching beanie facing the same snowstorm, only in this scenario, she’s not planning on braving it.

That’s the premise of “Let It Joy,” the brand’s Winter 2026 campaign. Stalter is stranded at Hotel Marc in downtown New York during a record-breaking blizzard when Mel Ottenberg, editor-in-chief of Interview knocks on her door with an invitation to a hotel holiday party. The catch: she never got the room number, and she has to hunt it down.

The imagery follows the party’s increasingly unhinged vignettes (and a lot of outfit changes), with a cast that’s a very New York who’s who: Knicks center Andre Drummond, social media personality Ashtin Earle, Mel Ottenberg, model and actress Kai Schreiber, and designer and stylist Miyako Bellizzi.

Marc Jacobs takes us on a humorous, glamorous, dreamlike ride of holiday gifting. Meg waltzes around in grandiose outerwear like The Puffer and slings around The Scene Bag, now in new sizes. Girl-world guests flaunt The Tote Bag in fresh poppy colorways alongside whimsical star-shaped balloons, running around the hotel in everything from the 72 Spring Street Sneaker to The Aspen Winter Boots. The Scene Wallet, small leather goods, accessories, and Marc Jacobs Beauty round out the gift-ready lineup.

The holiday dream world of Marc Jacobs has been built, and consider this your invitation. Part fantasy, part gift guide, and entirely worth joining. Just don’t forget to ask for the room number.

#6637. Taylor Swift Reveals the Cult Film Character She and Longtime Friend Abigail Have Been Impersonating Since They Were Teens

“It’s something our husbands have to put up with”

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Taylor Swift loves her pop culture references. After all, she named two of her cats after Grey’s Anatomy and Law & Order: SVU characters, her songs feature allusions to everything from Peter Pan to Romeo and Juliet, and she once even brought Lisa Kudrow on stage to do a rendition of “Smelly Cat” from Friends.

So, it comes as no surprise to learn that Swift is a secret fan of one of the biggest cult classic comedies of the early 2000s: Napoleon Dynamite. As it turns out, the movie was one of the first things that she and her longtime friend, Abigail Anderson, bonded over when they were teenagers.

This tidbit was revealed when Swift sat down for a rare Q&A with Toy Story 5 director Andrew Stanton yesterday afternoon, following a screening of the film in New York City. During their conversation, Swift noted how the relationship between the characters Bonnie and Blaze (voiced by Scarlett Spears and Mykal-Michelle Harris, respectively) mirrors that of her and Anderson’s friendship.

“I’d love to pile on to what Andrew was saying about finding someone who’s the same genre [of] weird and silly as you are and just why Bonnie and Blaze’s story resonated with me so much,” Swift shared.

“When I moved to Nashville when I was 14... you know, you’re the new kid in school and you’re like, ‘Who should I be friends with? These girls are cool, these girls are cool, these are nice girls,’” Swift recalled. “But there was one girl named Abigail—and she even has curly hair, too, like Blaze—and the two of us, all we wanted to do was talk in Napoleon Dynamite voices.”

Swift went on to reveal that this playful bonding exercise has continued long past their high school years. “And we still do this,” she said with a laugh. “And it’s something our husbands have to put up with.” (Swift is married to NFL tight end Travis Kelce, while Anderson is wed to a chief technology officer named Charles Berard.)

The two have been friends ever since they met in English class at Hendersonville High School in Tennessee, and Swift has referenced her BFF in songs like “Fifteen” and “Ruin the Friendship.” Anderson has even appeared in a number of Swift’s music videos, for tracks like “Picture to Burn” and “I’m Only Me When I’m With You.”

After sharing her special anecdote, Swift went on to do an impression of the titular Napoleon Dynamite character. Then, she tied it all back to Toy Story 5 by saying: “When you find that person who just completely sees you for the strange, little genre that is you at your purest, that hit me so hard watching the film.”

#6633. Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?

At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”

I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

#6631. Better American Sunscreens Are Here—But We’re Still Way Behind the Best

Anyone who’s applied sunscreen only to be left with a chalky white cast, a greasy finish knows American sun care has long been a frustrating experience. The US is decades behind European and Asian counterparts, which have long been blessed with sunscreens that are lighter, more luxurious, and easier to wear every day. For skincare obsessives (this writer included) trips abroad are also opportunities to stock up on superior sunscreens they can’t find at home.

The root of the problem is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration classifies sunscreen as a drug rather than a cosmetic. Because of that distinction, more time and testing is required to get new sunscreens on the shelves, dramatically reducing innovation in American sun protection. But for the first time since the ‘90s, we’ve had some movement on that front. In June of this year, the FDA approved a new sunscreen filter called bemotrizinol—also known as Tinosorb S or BEMT—after years of lobbying in the states by dermatologists, skincare brands, and Congress members. It’s a meaningful step toward better sun care, but the US is still lagging behind.

Bemotrizinol is prized for its ability to provide both UVA and UVB protection while remaining stable in sunlight. That’s a significant advantage over some existing US-approved filters, which offer protection against one type of UV radiation more effectively than the other. BEMT also has the potential to make sunscreen more pleasant to wear: “And because it’s a large, oil-loving molecule, it mostly stays on the surface of your skin instead of soaking in, and it blends into lightweight, non-greasy formulas with no white cast,” says Dr. Joel Spitz, co-founder, chief medical officer, and board-certified dermatologist at Honeydew, a virtual dermatology platform.

Bemotrizinol might be new for the US market, but it’s already been used in sunscreen formulations abroad for 20 years, Spitz says. That long track record helps explain why consumers in the US have spent years coveting the more cosmetically elegant formulas available in countries like South Korea and France. While most consumers would love if major brands like Neutrogena, La Roche-Posay, or Beauty of Joseon brought their European or Asian formulations to the US, those SPFs still contain filters that the FDA hasn’t approved. As a result, many brands are developing entirely new BEMT-centric formulas for use stateside.

Australian label Ultra Violette was the first brand to release a BEMT sunscreen in the US with its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in August 2026. Neutrogena debuted its Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 in September. Earlier this month French drugstore staple La Roche-Posay put its Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 up for sale online. Don’t mistake the relatively quick arrival of these products after the FDA’s approval for ease in which brands can develop new formulations. According to Emanuella Louis, La Roche-Posay’s public relations manager, the brand had been working on its new formula for more than two years.

That long lead time reflects the way sunscreen development works: Brands can research and test formulas in anticipation of regulatory changes, then move a product forward when a particular filter gets the green light. Louis says La Roche-Posay has access to filters the FDA may be considering for approval and is “actively working, playing, testing on what possibly those formulas would be.” When a filter is approved, she explains, a formula already in the testing pipeline can be moved up.

Some brands are still tinkering with BEMT formulas for the US. Round Lab, one of South Korea’s most popular sunscreen manufacturers, has sold a version of its SPF in the US since 2024, and is hard at work on a new version of those formulas that contains bemotrizinol.

“Bemotrizinol’s approval in the US is a meaningful change, but it does not mean a Korean formula can simply be brought to the US market as is,” says Koochul Kwon, Round Lab’s chief technology officer. Beyond incorporating the newly approved filter, brands must ensure the ingredients keep the UV filters stably dissolved and working alongside other components, including moisturizing ingredients. The finished product must then meet US requirements for SPF and broad-spectrum testing, product stability, and labeling. With those considerations in mind, Kwon expects Round Lab to release its own bemotrizinol sunscreen sometime in 2027.

A sunscreen is only as useful as a person’s willingness to wear it consistently. Bemotrizinol’s ability to protect against UV damage is important, but its potential to make formulas lighter, less greasy, and more comfortable could be just as consequential to get people to implement it in their everyday skincare routines.

“One of the strengths of Korean sun care is how naturally it has built sun protection into the everyday skincare experience,” Kwon says. “For people to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it when needed, the way it feels matters as much as how well it protects.”

But better filters alone won’t transform American sun care. The real breakthrough will be sunscreens that people actually enjoy wearing—and, as a result, are more likely to apply generously and reapply throughout the day, a key step to ensuring its effectiveness.

Charlotte Palermino, cofounder and chief brand officer of skincare brand Dieux, has been an advocate for easier sunscreen filter approvals ever since she tried her first Japanese sunscreen, Biore UV, a decade ago. She realized sunscreen could stave off skin issues after her dermatologist told her that her hyperpigmentation had been the result of failing to use sun protection. In the years since she has publicly pushed for regulatory reform. She’s hesitant to put an estimated release date on Dieux’s upcoming BEMT-centric sunscreen, simply because the brand is dialed in to ensure its able to deliver a quality, wearable product.

“We’ve gone through this with [Dieux’s] SkinMercy, which is an OTC colloidal oatmeal cream, but for sunscreen, the stability of your sunscreen is so fucking important,” she says. “If my sunscreen separates or if it’s not at that stated SPF 50, if that degrades at all with broad spectrum protection, I would be mortified.”

Palerimo cites brands like Korea’s Beauty of Joseon, which is more popular in the US than in its home country, as evidence that Americans have long been on the hunt for better sunscreen. And though BEMT is a step forward, we still have a way to go. Board-certified dermatologist Jane Yoo has been lobbying Congress to get new sunscreen filters approved for the US and is tracking the FDA’s progress in making those approvals. Currently there are seven other filters—bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane, octyl triazone, amiloxate, diethylhexyl butamido triazone iscotrizinol, ecamsule, and enzacamene—under the agency’s Time and Extent Application (TEA) pipeline. Those filters are part of the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act meant to speed up the process of determining if ingredients are Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective, or GRASE. But here we are 12 years later, and we’re still waiting for their approval.

“A good analogy is we’ve been making sunscreens with both of our hands tied behind our backs,” Palermino says. “We’ve now had one hand released. I would like both hands released.”

#6628. Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet

For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format.

Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes.

Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

#6625. Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake

Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days.

Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine.

Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes.

Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed.

Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly).

Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes.

Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely.

Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6624. 30 Gifts for Dads Who Swear They Don't Want Anything 2026

More often than not, finding the best gifts for dads involves putting your thinking cap on to mentally trawl through all of the very practical things they already own, along with the stuff that they’d just never use. Fortunately, we've got a few good dads on the GQ staff. Opinionated dads. Handsome dads. Great dads. And they've actually got some ideas.

Still no dice? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

Simple, generously proportioned, and blessed with a great collar, this checked shirt from Japanese label Frizmworks gets all the little things right. And the price? Legendary.

It's a good idea to pay closer attention to what's been happening at Filson lately. The brand's been digging into its archives and finding fresh ways to offer up its outdoorsmen roots, as evidenced by this Tacoma jacket, an old-school silhouette recast in a handsome denim.

There's a reason a Burberry check scarf costs what it does. The pattern is destined to outlast every passing trend and come back into fashion again and again. And the cashmere? Every bit as luxurious as he'd hope.

A Shaggy Dog for the shaggy ol' dog, y'know. J.Press's sweater is the real deal, made from Shetland wool that's hand-brushed to achieve its signature fuzzy texture. And yes, it's still made in Scotland, where the wool comes from. Tradition is tradition.

There's always a good reason for another pair of work boots, so why not make 'em Western? These meet the safety standards for commercial construction but look handsome as hell doing it.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

Of all the tech you could get him this year, a portable cassette player is probably the last thing he'd expect. This one comes from the nostalgia peddlers at Retrospekt. And if he doesn't appreciate the format, he'll at least appreciate the transparent casing that puts the inner circuitry on display.

Nocs Provisions is the first name in cool binoculars, and now it's got a lo-fi digital camera to match. It's a fun little shooter in its own right, but I love that you can take photos straight through a pair of binoculars or a monocular.

String 'em up or stake 'em in the ground—BioLite's solar-powered site lights make illuminating a campsite (or a backyard, balcony, or any outdoor area) a cinch. If he's a camper, he'll be a happy one.

#6622. The Author Behind the Pseudonym Rebecca Morrow Was a Total Mystery—Until Now

Rainbow Rowell is the bestselling writer behind the novel Corinne. Here, she explains why it was finally time to come forward.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In 2022, the novel Corinne was published. At the story’s center is Corinne, a woman who walked away from family and her fundamentalist upbringing but finds herself unable to forget Enoch, her first love. Rebecca Morrow, the name on the book’s cover, was described as a “pseudonym for a New York Times bestselling author,” and though readers guessed at who that author might be, Rebecca Morrow’s identity remained a mystery until now.

Rebecca Morrow is Rainbow Rowell, the celebrated author of Cherry Baby and Eleanor & Park, among others. Corinne isn’t about her life, but it has parallels, and in 2022, publishing something so personal felt impossible. Now denying what she has come to consider her favorite book seems unthinkable. In July 2027, Corinne will be reissued with Rowell’s name on the cover, and in 2028 she will publish Catch Us the Foxes, a Corinne sequel.

Here Rowell talks about the decision to write Corinne—and deciding to finally put her name on it—in her own words.

In the darkest hours of the COVID-19 pandemic—when the future seemed uncertain, and the rest of the world felt far away—I did something very strange for me.

I wrote a book, knowing that I couldn’t let anyone read it.

“I just need to do this,” I told my literary agent. “And then I’ll write something we can sell.” It was a good time to sell. I’d just published three No. 1 bestsellers in a row. “I just need to get this out of me first.”

I wrote the first draft of the novel almost feverishly. It was about a woman who is cast out of her strict Christian church as a teenager and cut off by her family. She comes back home as an adult to reckon with the past—and with the man who was the catalyst for her exile.

Really, the book was about all the things I’d always been too scared to write about, or even to talk about….Faith. Shame. Sex. (More sex. Unclean sex. Forbidden sex. Sex in the same room as a Bible.) And, most thornily, how it feels to leave a fundamentalist church. The way you eventually realize that you can’t leave. That you’ll always take it with you, because you were made there. Baked there. Poured and set.

When I was done with the manuscript, it was my favorite thing I’d ever written. Maybe not my best book, but already the one I loved the most.

“But honestly,” I told my agent, “we can’t do anything with this. It’s too personal. And it’s the very last thing any of my readers would want.” I was writing queer YA fantasy. Not whatever this was.

My agent, being an agent, asked if he could read it anyway.

And he liked it. (He liked my beautiful baby!)

We very quickly began talking about a way to publish the book that might sidestep all my fears and anxieties….

There began my strange—and still hardly believable to me—journey as Rebecca Morrow, the pseudonymous author of Corinne.

It was exciting at first. It was different and fun. A pseudonym! A secret identity! A way to drop a novel into the world without having to talk about it, or sell it. Without having to worry about alienating or recruiting my existing readers.

The pseudonym satisfied that still feverish part of me that needed to let the story out, but was too terrified to stand by it.

Oh, I knew it was absurd to write a book about shame and secrets, and then to keep it a secret. (Don’t think this didn’t come up in therapy!) But at the time, it seemed like the only path forward for Corinne. It was this or let the characters die on my hard drive.

My editor and I agonized over how to handle the pseudonym. Traditionally, authors write fake biographies to go with their fake names. But I didn’t want to get caught in a lie if I was found out. And I didn’t want to seek out undeserved goodwill as a “debut author.”

The marketing department really wanted something they could say about Rebecca Morrow. They suggested “lives in Nebraska,” but even that felt like divulging too much. We settled on “Rebecca Morrow is a pseudonym for a New York Times bestselling author.”

My apologies to the bestselling, usually Mormon, authors who got blamed for this weird book. I didn’t see that coming.

I did expect readers to guess that I was the author. Even though I’d freed myself to write Corinne in a new voice and shaken off some of my more recognizable habits, the book ended up sounding more like me than ever. It was like my voice distilled.

Some people did guess. It didn’t bother me. I still didn’t have to talk about the book. I didn’t have to face it.

Corinne is my favorite of my books and beyond that, Enoch and Corinne, the man and woman at its center, are my all-time favorite characters. It’s hard to explain why…

I always write messy, flawed characters, but these two are my messiest and most flawed. Their love is not the stuff of romance. (This novel is not a romance; it will disappoint you if you come to it looking for reassurance or escape.)

Neither Corinne nor Enoch is based on me, though they carry many of my burdens. This is not a hidden memoir. But they feel so real to me. They make mistakes, and I want to forgive them. I want them to find grace. I think about them still, all the time. I worry about what’s become of them.

Ultimately, that’s why I’m stepping forward to claim the book now. At some point, “not having to talk about Corinne” turned into “not being able to talk about Corinne,” even when I desperately wanted to.

I love this book! I want to put it on my shelf, between Any Way the Wind Blows and Scattered Showers. I want readers who liked Slow Dance and Cherry Baby to discover it.

I loved the characters in Corinne so much that I wrote a sequel about them—Catch Us the Foxes—and I want that book to have a life, too. William Morrow is launching both books, properly—Corinne next July, and Catch Us the Foxes in March 2028—in beautiful hardcover editions.

I revised Corinne for the new edition—I went a little deeper on the church stuff this time, and sharpened the focus on some of the characters. It’s a little longer. And, I think, a little better. My favorite designer, Jim Tierney, designed the new matching covers.

I still get a surge of fear and excitement every time I see my name there front and center.

My therapist says that I’m very good at compartmentalizing—keeping some parts of myself shut away from other parts. I would argue that this is a very useful skill! But it does bad things to your soul, over time...being fractured like that.

But as the years have passed, it’s felt like I’ve left something half done. Like Corinne is a truth half shared. A story half told. I needed to get the book out of me, but I ended up cutting myself off from it. That was never the goal.

I’m grateful to “Rebecca Morrow” for making Corinne possible, but I’m finally ready to bring these characters home.

#6621. Chickpea Saag

This take-out staple is easy enough to recreate at home and fantastic for family dinners. If you’re looking for a comforting vegetarian weeknight meal, this stripped-down version is the ticket—it takes little time to prep, is both budget- and pantry-friendly (thanks to frozen spinach and canned chickpeas), and always goes down a treat. If you have kasuri methi or dried fenugreek leaves, crumble a healthy pinch into the spinach when you’re blending the mixture. It’ll make the saag even more fragrant and delicious. Leftover saag, if any, tastes even better the next day.

Find more delicious vegetarian dinner ideas here: Gochujang-Butter-Braised Tofu; Crispy Tofu With Peanut Sauce; and Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms.

Melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium skillet with a lid over medium heat. Add 1 large white onion, thinly sliced, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, coarsely chopped, 2 tsp. cumin seeds, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and tender, 8–10 minutes.

Uncover pan and add ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ½ tsp. ground turmeric. Cook, stirring often, until yogurt is slightly thickened (it will split into tiny curds), about 2 minutes. Let cool a few minutes, then transfer to a blender; reserve skillet.

Add ½–1 serrano chile (depending on the spiciness of your chile and your heat preference), one 10-oz. package frozen spinach, thawed, and ½ tsp. garam masala to blender; blend until mixture is very smooth, about 3 minutes.

Return purée to reserved skillet and add one 15-oz. can chickpeas, rinsed. Cook saag over medium-low heat, stirring often, until heated through (do not bring to a simmer or saag may split).

Transfer saag to a medium bowl. Serve with steamed rice and/or warm naan, lime wedges, and more yogurt alongside.

Do Ahead: Saag can be made 1 day ahead. Let cool. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Reheat over medium-low heat before serving.

#6617. Dutch Apple Snacking Cake

Every autumn the siren song of baking calls bakers home until the volume becomes too much to bear. And at that moment, the only thing that can silence it is a warm-spiced apple cake—the kind that hugs you closer than a knit sweater. This recipe, which keeps things simple, relies on the winning combination of cinnamon and apples to perfume a vanilla cake with pockets of tender fruit. A blanket of cinnamon streusel crowns the cake, giving it a contrasting crunch and a coffee-cake-like character. Feel free to stash the cake on your counter, slicing it throughout the week, enjoying its plush interior as it magically gets better with time.

More cozy bakes this way: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Chocolate Olive Oil Cake; and Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly coat an 8x8" metal baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Lightly coat parchment with nonstick spray. Place 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (packed; 200 g) light brown sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, in a large bowl and mix with your hands, squeezing together as needed, until marble-size clumps form. Set streusel aside.

Toss 1 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 2 large), peeled, cored, thinly sliced, slices halved crosswise, and 2 Tbsp. (16 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to coat.

Whisk 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and remaining 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to combine. Add ½ cup (1 stick) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until no visible pieces remain. (Mixture should look like lightly moistened sand. Don’t worry about overworking it.) Add 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup buttermilk, 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract and stir until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Mix in about two thirds of apples.

Scrape batter into prepared pan and spread into an even layer; smooth surface. Scatter reserved streusel and remaining apples over, letting them organically intermix. Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 65–75 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan. Using parchment overhang, lift cake out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Dust with powdered sugar and cut into 12 pieces if serving immediately.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 5 days ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6616. 11 Best Men's Dress Shirts 2026, According to GQ Editors

Even if your closet is ninety percent fleece, the best men's dress shirts are non-negotiables. At some point, you’ll face an occasion that requires one—a laid-back wedding, a high-stakes job interview, a weirdly formal middle-school piano recital. But the right dress shirt won’t just save you in a pinch or help you sneak past upper management at your new corporate gig. (Especially if said corporate gig is working at GQ.)

Because the superlative versions of the style aren’t simply dress shirts—or, at least, not exclusively dress shirts. Buy one equipped with the right fit, details, and fabrics, and even the most formal of the bunch can kick it in less stuffy environments without eliciting snickers. We’re on-the-record fans of throwing one on with a groovy tie and crisp trousers, but toss a dress shirt over a graphic tee and baggy shorts, and suddenly, your otherwise schlubby fit looks exponentially more considered—and exponentially more stylish.

For starters, polos aren’t dress shirts just because they have a collar. We know, we know—finding the line between casual shirts and formal shirts is hard. Then there’s fabric, little details like cuffs, plackets, and color. And on top of all that, “the perfect fit” is so subjective. Take a deetp breath. We’ve got you. We’ve done the dirty work, buttoned more buttons than we thought was possible, aggregated a heap of our favorites, and wore ‘em every which way possible to determine, once and for all, the absolute best dress shirts for men.

We’ve wholeheartedly recommended J.Crew’s Bowery dress shirts for a long time. But it was up until just recently that the revered preppy label quietly released a new button-up that we had to do some internal reckoning. The Slim Portuguese cotton Oxford dress shirt doesn’t enjoy the distinction of being named after a New York City street (e.g. the Ludlow suit, or the 770 jeans). But don’t let the straight-forward, flavorless nomenclature fool you. Let’s start with the obvious: the fabric. It’s an all-cotton Oxford cloth woven exclusively for J.Crew by the respected Portuguese mill, Solemos. It’s smooth and luxurious with an elegant drape. Plus, the thicker yarns of an Oxford cloth makes it versatile enough for less formal occasions when you want to wear it with a pair of jeans, untucked, even.

It gets better from there. The shirt is a tastefully trimmed down to a silhouette that’s not skin-tight nor 2010s #menswear slim, but svelte enough to look clean without a blazer. But the real star of the show is that 10-out-of-10 collar. Most of J.Crew’s shirts are designed with wimpier collars that are likely, for better or worse, a product of those aforementioned #menswear times. This newcomer, however, extends it enough to a more classic size that bridges the blazer-collar gap so it sits neatly below a jacket lapel. That larger collar means it’s more proportional when paired with a tie.

We’re not a part of J.Crew’s internal meetings, but if anyone there is reading this, we think this needs to be expanded into more fabrics, colorways, and silhouettes—perhaps, it should even be dubbed with a new name.

If it comes as any surprise that Uniqlo sells one of the best bang-for-your-buck dress shirts on the market, you’re likely new to GQ Recommends—and the Japanese retailer’s assortment of eminently affordable men’s clothing staples. Unlike its Calvin Klein counterpart, Uniqlo’s riff on the genre isn’t available with the added benefit of Prime shipping, but what you get instead is a dress shirt that’s worth exponentially more than what you pay for.

You might only go to Uniqlo for the basics—tees, underwear, socks, maybe a hoodie. So I'd understand if you thought dress shirts were too refined a category for Uniqlo to be any good. But every I time I encounter a dress shirt from the Japanese retailer, I'm reminded of just how surprisingly solid its fits and construction are. Unlike most of its price-conscious competition, Uniqlo’s dress shirt is made from 100% long-staple cotton with absolutely zero stretch involved. While you might think of a little elastane as a good thing, generally speaking, it tends to mean that corners were cut. Plus, if a dress shirt fits well, you won't need any stretch.

The fabric is treated for wrinkle resistance, which is great if you're the kind of guy who has a “clothes chair”. But there's a funny sort of sheen that comes with wrinkle-resistant shirts that can be off-putting. That said, the details redeem it completely: no sloppy stitching, exposed seams, or wimpy collars here. Perhaps most crucially, the slim fit isn’t so svelte that you’ll look like you got dressed in 2010.

Both our overall pick and budget pick are solid options no matter your budget or snobbery. But if you're ready to graduate or just feeling like skipping ahead to the finer things, Todd Snyder's line of in-house shirting is where we'd point you. A great dress shirt starts with great fabric and Mr. Snyder's collection is full of top-notch poplins, twills, and broadcloths sourced from Thomas Mason, a revered mill that's been around since 1796 and have been the go-to for grail shirtmakers like Turnbull & Asser, not to mention the Royal family.

In the hands of American menswear nobility, the fabrics are given that distinct yet trend-averse Todd Snyder flavor. It's cut with a tastefully slim silhouette that's not Slimane-skinny, but not what your dad thinks of as skinny, either. The back features comfy side pleats, which are sewn into a split yoke (a fairly uncommon, but appreciated detail for the menswear nerds). Fine stitching and single-needle construction throughout, the shirt is built with a ton of delectable details for stylishly discerning, but what we love most is the extended collar. It's a detail that feels refreshing but also recalls shirts from the 1930s, arguably a golden age for tailoring in the States.

This beauty will run you a bit over $200, which ain't nothing. But that's a resonable sum compared to the heritage shirtmakers whose reputations have been built on shirting alone. Often, their shirts can cost you as much as your car's mortgage. That said, Todd Snyder's will get you like, 90% of the way there for a third of the price.

Got a last-minute invite to a swanky event and need a dress shirt ASAP? Not to fear, Amazon is here (and there, and pretty much everywhere). Calvin Klein’s no-frills slim fit shirt is cut from high-quality cotton that’s just a tad more stretchy than our overall pick, and comes equipped with plenty of next-gen specs its counterparts eschew—including moisture-wicking properties to keep you cool and a non-iron coating to keep it looking crisp. (You’re short on time, right?) Mercifully, the added spandex offers a little give without making the shirt look too shiny.

Throw it over your finest chinos or the dress pants you impulsively splurged on or wear it with jeans on a relaxed Friday in the office. Even if you bought it at the eleventh hour, it won’t take long for it to supplant the pricier competition.

When you’re rolling with the movers and shakers of the world, you need a dress shirt that can keep up. And that’s exactly what the vaunted Parisian chemise-makers at Charvet specialize in, to the delight of royalty both literal (countless French kings) and cultural (Sofia Coppola is a well-known fan). This breezy cotton number is no exception: It’s cut on the looser side and features an extremely classy double cuff for when you're ready to break out the cufflinks you inherited from your old man. Even with the tres formale flourishes, though, we wouldn't shy away from rocking it in a more casual context. When you slip on this sucker, you don’t need to meet with the boss—you are the boss.

“Charvet does not fuck around,” Grossman says bluntly. There’s no shortage of reasons why it remains the first name in old-world dress shirts—and its centuries of pedigree barely cracks the top five. Sure, the brand has outfitted kings, presidents, and titans of industry in equal number, but its core value proposition comes down to one exceedingly simple principle: uncompromising quality. Every dress shirt is still made by hand in Charvet’s wood-paneled Parisian townhouse, which is worth the cost of a flight to visit, Grossman notes.

If you’re not quite ready to drop half a grand on a dress shirt your grandkids will fight over, he also recommends a more wallet-friendly hack: These days, Charvet’s shirts are all over the vintage market, and “you can reliably score one for a lot less than retail”.

Proper Cloth’s been an open secret to menswear heads for years thanks to its surprisingly granular made-to-order service which offers a wide range of custom options from fabric to design details to sizing. Beyond the near-bespoke service, Proper Cloth’s quality will turn the heads of the keen-eyed tailoring nerds. 80s two-ply pinpoint fabric made from American Supima cotton, split yoke construction, and a handsome semi spread collar all come together for one of the best dress shirts you can get for the price.

One of the most compelling arguments we’ve seen in favor of dressing up right now comes straight from Paris, where Husbands outfits its worldly clientele in exquisite dress shirts exactly like this, a masterclass in retro ‘70s swagger so good it clinched a spot in GQ’s inaugural All-Stars class. It looks rad unbuttoned to the navel, and even groovier with a hefty foulard tie.

One of the best things about a cutaway collar? It gives you more room for a declaratively large tie knot.

The J.Crew pick up top is incredible. But it's slim. This Ludlow dress shirt has all the same reliability, but is also cut to a fuller shape.

Given the brand’s stellar reputation in the tailoring place, it shouldn’t come as a shock that Sid Mashburn hawks a grip of bang-up dress shirts, too. This bengal stripe number is a tried-and-true riff on a traditional office-ready pattern, but the spread collar and Goldilocks cut imbue it with Mahsburn’s signature Southern charm—and yank it firmly into 2025.

While this nicely-priced shirt does also come in white, it's also a good reminder that dress shirts can still have some edge, too.

As with any garment, “good” is subjective—but as a general rule of thumb, it comes down to three crucial factors: fabric, construction, and fit. Men’s dress shirts are no different. Michael Hill, Creative Director of Drake’s says, “Versatility is important. Customers need to understand fabric and context. For instance, Oxford cotton is going to be more versatile than poplin, which is typically a bit more formal.” The fabric will help dictate the occasion (or the other way around?). There are so many at your disposal from herringbone to end-on-end to pinpoint, not to mention stripes to plaids. So if you’re not sure, ask the sales staff.

Hill also emphasizes that fit is essential to a good dress shirt and to pay attention to the details like “The way the collar sits on your neck and against the body of the shirt. Does it stay tucked in throughout the day? How do the cuffs sit against the wrist?”

He goes on to give this absolute, “Great dress shirts are never made from synthetic or stretch fabrics.” The majority of good dress shirts eschew synthetic materials in favor of natural long-staple cotton, woven tightly for extra durability. Cotton, of course, is not a prerequisite—but almost every single great dress shirt we’ve swaddled our torsos in has been made from some riff on the fabric, from poplin to pinpoint Oxford cloth.

Other reliable indicators of quality shirts? Telltale details like French or felled seams, which are sleeker and more durable; mother of pearl buttons; and a denser or finer stitch count, usually commensurate with the amount of craftsmanship involved. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth also notes to look out for less common details like reinforced shirt tail gussets, a split yoke, tight and straight stitching, and emphasizes the importance of buttons. “Are the buttons shanked so they won’t come loose? Are the buttons a durable enough material that can withstand your cleaners repeatedly?” These small details reveal whether a shirtmaker is paying close attention.

One unique difference between dress shirts and other garments comes down to the collar. Skerritt says the collar “often has the largest impact on how the shirt makes you look.” That’s because it frames your face and interacts with directly with your suit jacket and its lapels—no small job for a garment. While Skerritt advises to look for fusing (the way that the collar is attached or glued to its interlining) that’s crisp, and a collar that stands up well around the neck, ultimately it “should look natural and effortless. The end result should be [that] you like how it makes you feel in the way that you like to dress.”

As any menswear wonk will tell you, dress shirts boast no shortage of nuances. So in the name of brevity (and general wonk-avoidance), we compiled a handy-dandy glossary to the terms you’ll encounter most often. As a rule of thumb, the less adornment a dress shirt has, the more formal it is.

Like all of menswear, collars are susceptible to the whims of the trend cycle, swelling and shrinking with any given era’s silhouettes du jour. Collar sizes are prone to change, too (see: the massive collars of the power-suited ‘80s; the ultra-shrunken collars of the indie-sleaze 2010s). These are the three you should know.

Cuffs are the small pieces of additional fabric at the end of the shirt sleeve; they're often constructed with stiffer linings to give them structure and thoroughly cover your wrists. These are the two you should know.

Plackets are the strip of fabric that runs down the front of the shirt, designed to be fastened with buttons, snaps, or zippers. (When it comes to dress shirts, you’ll almost always encounter the former.) These are the three you should know.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

If you ask us, animal print should be considered a neutral: a pattern so timeless and versatile, it deserves a permanent home in your forever wardrobe, alongside those blue jeans, white tees, and black boots.

And while zebra stripes and cheetah spots may come and go, there’s no more ubiquitous animal pattern than leopard print. Since its 1980s heyday, fashion’s perennial favorite has been reimagined countless times, leaning either ultra-glam or rebelliously punk, depending on how you wear it.

But for FW26, the spots are finally changing. While we’re absolutely not decreeing the demise of leopard (our love will never wane), there’s now a new pattern breathing fresh life into our autumnal wardrobes.

Deer print—or, to use its other moniker, Bambi print—is the pattern to know this season, appearing across ready-to-wear and accessories from one end of the street to the other. The easiest entry route may be a pair of calf-hair ballet flats or a working-week tote, but the most impactful approach? That has to be Mango’s stellar pair of balloon-leg jeans, which are destined to replace that leopard-print pair we know you were wearing all weekend long.

With a voluminous curved leg, this frankly excellent pair of statement jeans ticks off two major FW26 trends in one—and they’re incredibly flattering to boot (if you haven’t tried this silhouette yet, now’s the time). Priced at $90, they’re already selling out fast, so we suggest you move swiftly.

What to wear them with? Really, the options are plentiful. All the classics will work here: your white T-shirt, gray cardigan, cozy black sweater. Leather looks particularly chic—consider a funnel-neck jacket or slick black accessories. Sneakers and color-pop socks are your weekend go-to, of course. For smarter occasions, a dark taupe-brown lipstick will lend the look a little glamour, as will a pair of chunky silver earrings. And on your feet? Ballet flats now (a pointed style is an especially good move) and block-heel boots once the cold really sets in.

#6613. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Adding cottage cheese to a meatball might sound like an attempt to cram extra protein into a recipe, but it’s not the only valid reason. Something magical happens with the addition of cottage cheese: It practically disappears in the baking process, lending the meatballs juiciness and a subtle savory-salty flavor. As a bonus, the cottage cheese helps to stretch the recipe and you’ll end up with almost twice as many meatballs from one pound of ground beef.

Think of this recipe as a bit of a blank canvas, allowing you to use the meatballs however you please. You can bake them and pop them in your mouth as is, drop them into simmering tomato sauce, or stuff them between slices of bread for a hearty sandwich. They, like most meatballs, are also very meal-prep-friendly and take to freezing well.

More great cottage cheese recipes this way: Cottage Cheese Lasagna; Cottage Cheese Caramelized Onion Dip; and Roasted Honeynut Squash With Cottage Cheese and Chili Crisp.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Mix together 1 large egg, 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, one 16-oz. container cottage cheese, 1 lb. ground beef, 1 cup Italian breadcrumbs, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large bowl to combine. Scoop out into 2-Tbsp. (heaping) portions and roll into smooth balls between your hands (you should have about 30).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large nonstick skillet over high heat. Working in batches and adding more oil between batches as needed, cook meatballs in a single layer, turning halfway through, until browned on 2 sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet and bake in oven until cooked through, 12–14 minutes.

Do Ahead: Meatballs can be made 3 days ahead. Let cool; transfer to an airtight container and chill, or freeze up to 1 month.

#6612. Zendaya Recreated an Iconic Halle Berry Fashion Moment for Halloween

Zendaya didn’t miss out on all the fun this Halloween. The actress dressed up as one of Hollywood’s most enduring screen and style icons, Halle Berry, thanks to a special vintage pull.

On Saturday, Zendaya’s longtime stylist, Law Roach, shared a series of photos of the Dune actress recreating a particularly memorable early-aughts look that Berry wore: a butter yellow, brown, and white printed string bikini top with silver accents and matching low-rise, wide-leg trousers from Lanvin’s fall 2000 collection. Zendaya completed the look with pointed-toe heels.

Roach thanked Lanvin’s artistic director Peter Copping and Alix Long in his post. Copping took the creative reins at the French fashion house in 2024, and Cristina Ortiz was Lanvin’s womenswear designer when the fall 2000 collection debuted.

Berry first wore the two-piece to the New York premiere of X-Men in July 2000. She accessorized with a belly chain and tinted sunglasses.

Berry saw the tribute and posted her approval on X. “She won,” Berry wrote of Zendaya.

The fashion homage feels particularly fitting given that Zendaya has been drawing comparisons to Berry since debuting her pixie cut.

In fact, when Zendaya first unveiled the look at the 2026 Emmy Awards in September, Roach confirmed that the haircut was inspired by Berry’s iconic short hairstyle.

Berry later embraced the tribute, sharing Roach’s interview on her Instagram Story and writing that Zendaya “murdered the night.”

This isn’t the first time Zendaya has used fashion to pay tribute to another star. In 2013, she channeled the late Aaliyah for Keep a Child Alive’s Dream Halloween, recreating the singer’s iconic Tommy Hilfiger campaign look. More recently, she honored Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in a vintage Bob Mackie design.

Zendaya and Roach have more fashion moments ahead: The actress’s Dune: Part Three press tour is just kicking off.
